articles.title: Numerical analysis of dynamics between debris flows and wave propagation using multi-layer shallow water equations
articles.titleEn: Numerical analysis of dynamics between debris flows and wave propagation using multi-layer shallow water equations
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: Debris flows are destructive disasters that often cause casualties and property damage, particularly when occurring near residential areas. In reservoir basins, debris flows can reduce effective storage capacity by raising the dead storage level and generate waves that may induce overtopping or structural collapse. Previous numerical studies have applied three-dimensional (3D) hydrodynamics or smoothed particle hydrodynamics to analyze debris flow-induced waves. However, these studies focused on the direct inflow of soil masses into water, without accounting for erosion and entrainment processes. As a result, they have limitations in simulating debris generated in upland areas that undergo erosion and entrainment before entering reservoirs. To address this gap, we developed a one-dimensional (1D) multi-layer simulation model based on shallow water equations that explicitly considers erosion, entrainment, and deposition. The model was validated through theoretical analysis and a laboratory experiment, and applied to the 2020 Sanyang Reservoir collapse event in South Korea. Scenario-based simulations were performed under varying debris flow characteristics and reservoir water levels. The results demonstrate that debris flow momentum strongly correlates with the scale of generated waves, with maximum momentum serving as a reliable predictor of wave magnitude. This study offers a practical framework for assessing debris flow impacts on dam and reservoir safety.

articles.title: COHESION: a connectivity-based framework for evaluating landslide susceptibility, runout hazards, and hillslope–channel coupling
articles.titleEn: COHESION: a connectivity-based framework for evaluating landslide susceptibility, runout hazards, and hillslope–channel coupling
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: Landslides hinder sustainable development in mountain regions by threatening livelihoods and damaging linear and water infrastructure. Susceptibility maps are widely used to identify landslide hazards, yet they usually omit hillslope connectivity. This is a critical shortcoming for mapping the magnitude of landslides, for identifying cascading hazards, and for understanding landslide contributions to fluvial sediment budgets. We introduce COHESION (COnnected HillslopE SusceptibIlity for slOpe failure and ruNout), a framework for coupling pixel-level susceptibility mapping approaches with connectivity analysis to identify downslope-connected landslide objects (LSOs), associated runout pathways and runout intersections with river networks. For the 7573 km 2 Kaligandaki Basin in Nepal, we base COHESION on a factor-of-safety assessment with probabilistic rainfall forcing and identify 1.06 million potential LSOs. Of these, 690 000 LSOs have nonzero precipitation-exceedance probabilities and cover 31.0 % of the basin. Precipitation-exceedance probabilities imply an annualized failure potential equivalent to 4.9 % of the basin area. Based on these probabilities, we propose that sediment mobilization from landsliding is constrained by soil-production and soil-mantle recovery rates rather than by triggering rainfall, a constraint hidden by typical susceptibility maps that do not account for failure volumes and probabilities. Considering runout pathways increases the mapped landslide-hazard footprint by 53.3 %. 29.7 % of buildings and 66.8 % of road segments are located on LSOs, while 20.7 % of buildings and 16.3 % of roads are on runout pathways. 35.3 % of LSOs connect to the river network, linking slope failures and river channels at more than 30 000 locations. Both results highlight the need to include connectivity and runout in geohazard screening and fluvial sediment budgets. COHESION's connectivity-based approach can improve the basin-scale screening of landslide hazards to settlements, roads, and water infrastructure, while also linking slope failure to sediment delivery in mountain rivers.

articles.title: Sequential anion chemistry enables dynamic interphase regulation in high-voltage LiCoO 2
articles.titleEn: Sequential anion chemistry enables dynamic interphase regulation in high-voltage LiCoO 2
articles.abstract: Lithium-ion batteries using LiCoO 2 cathodes have powered portable electronics for decades, yet their operation above 4.5 volts remains severely constrained by the unstable evolution of the cathode-electrolyte interphase (CEI). Under high-voltage conditions, lattice oxygen release and continuous electrolyte oxidation progressively degrade interfacial integrity. Here, we report a diluent-mediated local solvation regulation strategy to decrease dissociative solvent molecules and induce dual anion selective redistribution around Li + , forming a sequential solvation motif that drives sequential anion interfacial chemistry. DFOB − preferentially decomposes to establish a robust initial CEI framework, while BF 4 − continuously drives interfacial reactions to dynamically repair CEI defects and quench reactive oxygen species generated from lattice oxygen release. This dynamic regulation mechanism effectively stabilizes LiCoO 2 under aggressive high-voltage cycling. Consequently, the LiCoO 2 cathode delivers stable performance for 500 cycles at 4.5 volts with 73.5% capacity retention even in a low-concentration ether-based electrolyte. Furthermore, graphite||LiCoO 2 pouch cell achieves an energy density of 265.8 watt-hours per kilogram and exhibits favorable low-temperature resilience, retaining 99.1% capacity after 700 cycles at −20°C. These findings provide critical mechanistic insights into how solvation structure–driven anion chemistry can govern interfacial stability and unlock high-voltage, extreme-condition lithium-ion batteries.

articles.title: DFT-assisted natural abundance 13 C zero-field NMR via optical magnetometry
articles.titleEn: DFT-assisted natural abundance 13 C zero-field NMR via optical magnetometry
articles.abstract: Zero-field (ZF) nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy probes nuclear J-couplings without homogeneous magnetic fields, enabling inexpensive and geometrically flexible detection, including through metal. However, its broader use for chemical analysis has been limited by sensitivity and the difficulty of predicting the dense ZF multiplets. Here we demonstrate natural-abundance (1.1%) carbon-13 ( 13 C) ZF spectroscopy on off-the-shelf liquids using a compact commercial rubidium-87 magnetometer without hyperpolarization or special preparation. Instrumental advances yield improved sensitivity, ≤250-millihertz linewidths, and >week-long stability, enabling isotopomer-resolved fingerprint spectra across a 13-molecule library, including rare (0.0121%) doubly 13 C-labeled species. In parallel, we demonstrate vibrationally corrected density functional theory (DFT) prediction of ZF spectra with good qualitative agreement. Comparing experiment with these calculations renders residual deviations as chemically informative, reporting on hydrogen bonding and ion pairing at high ionic strength. These results contribute toward DFT-assisted ZF NMR as a general platform for field constraint–free molecular identification and for extracting transient solution-state structure from responsive J-coupling observables.

articles.title: Interband connectivity and climate shaped Neanderthal extinction and Homo sapiens ’ dispersal
articles.titleEn: Interband connectivity and climate shaped Neanderthal extinction and Homo sapiens ’ dispersal
articles.abstract: To what extent Neanderthal extinction was triggered by climate change or the arrival of Homo sapiens , and by which mechanisms, remains unresolved. Here, on the basis of climate-driven changes in habitat favorability for primary and secondary consumers and in net primary productivity, we estimate carrying capacity, herbivore biomass, and intraguild predation pressure during the time Neanderthals and H. sapiens lived in Europe. These spatially explicit estimates were incorporated into an agent-based model simulating human demographic dynamics under various scenarios. Results indicate that carrying capacity changes cannot explain Neanderthal extinction at a continental scale, though they are essential to understanding spatiotemporal distribution patterns of both human species. Conversely, the arrival of H. sapiens remarkably increased Neanderthal extinction likelihood. Because of the successive demographic expansions and contractions, group connectivity emerges as the key factor shaping population stability in both species. These findings support that Neanderthal disappearance and H. sapiens dispersals were interconnected demographic processes.

articles.title: Environment-adaptive molecular neural networks enabled by heterogeneous threshold DNA neuron
articles.titleEn: Environment-adaptive molecular neural networks enabled by heterogeneous threshold DNA neuron
articles.abstract: Molecular neural networks enable autonomous information processing in biochemical environments, yet most existing DNA-based implementations operate with fixed connectivity after assembly, limiting their ability to adapt network topology to changing environments. Here, we report an environment-adaptive molecular neural network enabled by DNA neurons with sequence-programmed, heterogeneous activation thresholds. These neurons incorporate triplex-based proton-gated DNA switches with tunable pH-response windows, which regulate the accessibility of toehold and recognition domains to switch pre-encoded weighted connections between inactive and signal-propagating states, thereby reconfiguring network connectivity without changing molecular composition. We demonstrate this principle in a DNA neural network that processes 64-bit inputs, where environmental acidification activates dormant neurons and reconfigures the computational topology from a sparse convolutional neural network for coarse two-class categorization into a fully connected neural network for fine-grained discrimination among four distinct patterns. Our results establish DNA-based neural circuits capable of adapting their computational architecture to environmental cues, offering a framework for molecular information processing in fluctuating biochemical environments.

articles.title: Enzymatic degradation of a polyester-based thermoset composite resin by an engineered cutinase from Fusarium solani
articles.titleEn: Enzymatic degradation of a polyester-based thermoset composite resin by an engineered cutinase from Fusarium solani
articles.abstract: Thermoset composites have become indispensable high-performance materials across key industrial sectors. However, existing recycling methods have yet to deliver sustainable end-of-life solutions for these materials. Here, we report the engineering of a highly active and stable biocatalyst capable of depolymerizing polyester-based thermoset composites. First, a second-generation polyester resin was designed to enhance susceptibility to enzymatic attack. Cutinase from Fusarium solani was selected and subsequently engineered through a combination of directed evolution and computational design using two soluble surrogate motifs representative of the redesigned resin structure. The resulting variant, which incorporated 19 mutations, exhibited a 22-fold increase in activity and an 11°C improvement in melting temperature while achieving recombinant production titers at the gram-per-liter scale in yeast cultivated in fed-batch bioreactor. This engineered enzyme depolymerized the polyester resin with a total release of 6 mM (∼1.08 grams per liter) monomethyl phthalate. Together, to our knowledge, these findings constitute the first documented example of enzymatic degradation of a complex polyester resin from thermoset composite materials.

articles.title: Resolving the black hole sphere of influence in a hyperluminous obscured quasar at redshift 4.6
articles.titleEn: Resolving the black hole sphere of influence in a hyperluminous obscured quasar at redshift 4.6
articles.abstract: Supermassive black holes (SMBHs) imprint gravitational signatures on the matter within their sphere of influence (SoI). Nuclear gas dynamics can hence be used to accurately measure the mass of an SMBH, yet these measurements remain elusive in the early universe. We report the first dynamical measurement of an SMBH mass at z > 2, based on high–spatial resolution observations of the ionized-carbon 157.7-micrometer and carbon monoxide (12-11) 216.93-micrometer emission lines that resolve the SoI in an obscured quasar at z = 4.6. The radial profile of the velocity dispersion reveals a clear Keplerian rise, requiring the presence of an ∼6 × 10 9 –solar mass SMBH. We propose that heavily obscured quasars allow such tracers to survive in the inner regions and may be ideal targets for increasing dynamical SMBH mass estimates in the early universe.

articles.title: A state-dependent neural circuit resolves approach-avoidance conflict
articles.titleEn: A state-dependent neural circuit resolves approach-avoidance conflict
articles.abstract: To survive, animals must balance opportunity and risk, yet how internal motivational state biases this trade-off remains poorly understood. Here, we show that hunger gates avoidance of a noxious stimulus in Drosophila to enable food approach under conflict. Using a behavioral assay in which flies must cross an electric shock barrier to reach food, we find that starvation promotes shock tolerance only when food-related olfactory cues are present. This state- and context-dependent behavioral shift is mediated by a defined neuromodulatory circuit. Leucokinin neurons encode hunger and convey this information to PV5K1 lateral horn output neurons, which integrate internal state signals with food odor cues and suppress shock-responsive FB2B neurons in the ventral fan-shaped body. Accordingly, electric shock-evoked activity in FB2B neurons is suppressed in starved flies exposed to food cues. articles.title: Spheroid-laden hydrogels with dual biomimetic intra- and perispheroidal niches for enhanced bone healing
articles.titleEn: Spheroid-laden hydrogels with dual biomimetic intra- and perispheroidal niches for enhanced bone healing
articles.abstract: Stem cell spheroid–hydrogel platforms offer promise for bone defect repair, but implantation-associated oxidative stress, poor vascular ingrowth, and insufficient osteogenic cues limit their clinical translation. Here, we developed dual-NICHE (dual niche-instructive construct for bone healing and engraftment), a gelatin methacryloyl hydrogel containing human adipose–derived stem cell spheroids with spatially distinct intra-/perispheroidal niches. Within a single construct, these two niches provide complementary functions to simultaneously address the key bottlenecks in bone regeneration. The intraspheroidal niche incorporated bone morphogenetic protein-2–immobilized fibers to promote osteogenic differentiation, whereas the perispheroidal matrix contained Sr 2+ –tannic acid nanoparticles (NPs). Upon implantation, the NPs mitigated oxidative stress and supported vascular infiltration. Concurrently, the osteogenic cue promoted differentiation, while the NPs facilitated mineral nucleation and growth, as further supported by molecular dynamics simulations. Together, this spatial integration enhanced vascularized bone formation with a bone volume fraction of ∼13.5% using only 5208 cells per defect in a mouse calvarial model, providing a potentially translatable framework for bone regeneration.

articles.title: Seasonal effects of simulated marine heatwaves on temperature-dependent growth performance
articles.titleEn: Seasonal effects of simulated marine heatwaves on temperature-dependent growth performance
articles.abstract: Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are increasingly longer and more frequent globally, but the cumulative impacts of multiple events on organism performance remain poorly understood. Using thermal performance models, we simulate the effects of simple seasonal MHW scenarios on the predicted growth of 36 mariculture species across the western Pacific Ocean. Simulations suggested that winter MHWs could generally benefit growth, while summer MHWs produced generally negative impacts, especially at higher latitudes where species experience summer growth periods. When combined, winter and summer MHW scenarios indicated a cumulative negative effect for most species. Vulnerability was highest at the warm- and cold-range edges of species’ distributions. These simulations suggest that temperature-dependent growth may be closely linked to the seasonal timing and frequency of extreme events, with multi-season MHWs posing potential challenges for mariculture species in the future. Our simulations highlight the importance of considering multi-season impacts in climate adaptation strategies.

articles.title: GenNA: Conditional generation of nucleotide sequences guided by natural language annotations
articles.titleEn: GenNA: Conditional generation of nucleotide sequences guided by natural language annotations
articles.abstract: Deciphering the mapping between biomolecular sequences and complex biological functions is a central challenge in genomics. While existing generative nucleotide models capture sequence distributions, they lack explicit access to gene-associated biological semantics, limiting semantics-guided design. Here, we present GenNA, a generative nucleotide foundation model guided by natural language annotations. Pretrained on a multimodal nucleotide-text corpus spanning 2221 eukaryotic species (∼416 billion characters), GenNA internalizes relationships between sequence syntax and functional semantics within a unified autoregressive framework. Without explicit rule-based supervision, GenNA yields distinguishable perplexity responses to sequence-annotation mismatches, mutational variants, and species-label perturbations. Furthermore, across diverse generation tasks, GenNA produces statistically plausible nucleotide sequences consistent with target semantics, structural constraints, and species contexts. Overall, GenNA provides a versatile framework for controllable nucleotide generation, establishing a practical route to integrate functional descriptions with sequence design.

articles.title: Assessing Regional Projections of Marine Climatic Impact‐Drivers Using Coordinated Ensembles: Framework and Application to the Mediterranean Sea
articles.titleEn: Assessing Regional Projections of Marine Climatic Impact‐Drivers Using Coordinated Ensembles: Framework and Application to the Mediterranean Sea
articles.abstract: The Mediterranean Sea is among the most climate‐sensitive regions globally, having experienced unprecedented sea surface temperatures, intensified marine heatwaves, and associated ecosystem impacts in recent years. These changes are projected to intensify throughout the 21st century, with implications for marine ecosystems, biogeochemical processes, and coastal societies. Here, we provide a transferable framework for assessing marine climatic impact‐drivers (CIDs) based on key physical ocean essential climate variables, integrating model evaluation, simulation filtering, and confidence assessment of projected changes across global warming levels. The framework is applied to the Mediterranean Sea using a coordinated ensemble of 29 multi‐decadal simulations from high‐resolution regional climate system models participating in Med‐CORDEX. A novel set of marine CIDs is assessed across warming levels from 1.5°C to 4°C, encompassing mean and extreme ocean temperature, mean ocean salinity, vertical stratification, and wind‐driven ocean dynamics at basin, sub‐basin, and coastal scales. Overall, model responses broadly align with historical trends, increasing confidence in projected changes. Projections indicate robust increases in mean ocean temperature, warm extremes, and stratification across regions as warming intensifies. Under high warming levels, extreme warm events become near‐yearly occurrences, whereas cold spells virtually disappear. In contrast, projected changes in salinity, wind stress extremes, and coastal upwelling remain comparatively uncertain across most regions. Beyond the Mediterranean, the proposed framework provides a consistent basis for assessing marine climate risks in other regions as high‐resolution regional projections become available, while remaining adaptable to new indicators. To facilitate the exploration of Mediterranean CID projections, an interactive web tool is provided.

articles.title: Advancing Sub‐Surface Hydrology Through WRF‐Hydro/MODFLOW Coupling: Interface Structure and Showcase Demonstration
articles.titleEn: Advancing Sub‐Surface Hydrology Through WRF‐Hydro/MODFLOW Coupling: Interface Structure and Showcase Demonstration
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: Conventional land surface models (LSMs) have evolved to represent detailed physics for many aspects of water flow and transport but still suffer from missing/simplified processes at the (lower) subsurface boundary. These gaps limit ability to simulate sub‐surface and surface water and energy fluxes. We present a dynamic framework for coupling of the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) MODFLOW, an open‐source hydrologic model representing subsurface hydrology, to WRF‐Hydro, a predominantly surface‐water‐focused hydrologic modeling system. The Basic Model Interface (BMI) coupling standard is used to communicate information between the hydrologic process components of WRF‐Hydro (i.e., the Noah‐Multiparameterization (Noah‐MP) and surface routing modules) and the MODFLOW groundwater component. The BMI functions initialize WRF‐Hydro and MODFLOW simulations, update model states and fluxes (passing groundwater recharge and discharge between WRF‐Hydro and MODFLOW), and finalize the run. The USGS National Groundwater Model, a calibrated steady‐state MODFLOW model, is used as the baseline groundwater model in simulations. The new coupled WRF‐Hydro/MODFLOW model is tested over the Republican and Delaware River basins, contrasting test beds with different climates and surface water‐groundwater coupling and complexities. The dynamics of the coupled framework are assessed through tracking changes in hydrologic processes. Two‐way WRF‐Hydro/MODFLOW coupling increased deep‐soil moisture retention and surface evapotranspiration, particularly in low‐relief areas. Groundwater dynamics were largely controlled by transient recharge from WRF‐Hydro highlighting the value of integrated modeling for capturing spatiotemporal hydrologic variability. This modeling effort seeks to advance the representation of groundwater in land and hydrological models and to improve the quantification of groundwater‐soil‐atmosphere and groundwater‐surface water interactions.

articles.title: Comparative Evaluation of Low‐Flow Estimation Performance in Noah‐MP for Improved Hydrological Modeling Across the United States
articles.titleEn: Comparative Evaluation of Low‐Flow Estimation Performance in Noah‐MP for Improved Hydrological Modeling Across the United States
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: Accurately simulating low flows is essential for effective water resource management and ecosystem conservation. This study evaluates five runoff and groundwater configurations in the Noah‐MP land surface model—SIMGM, SIMTOP, Schaake96, BATS, and the newly integrated Groundwater for Ungauged Basins (GrUB)—across 543 minimally disturbed reference basins in the contiguous United States. GrUB represents groundwater discharge using a representative‐hillslope formulation with independently derived watershed‐scale parameters and no basin‐specific streamflow calibration. Model performance was assessed using Kling‐Gupta Efficiency (KGE), Nash‐Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and bias under general and low‐flow conditions, identified by the 80% exceedance flows () and Tennant method (). Results indicate no configuration performed best across all metrics. During low‐flow periods, Schaake96 consistently produced the lowest MAE and bias, while GrUB generally ranked second and outperformed SIMGM, SIMTOP, and BATS under both low‐flow definitions. Over the full simulation period, GrUB showed comparatively strong overall performance and the lowest median bias. Spatially, the five configurations generally overestimated low flows in many central and eastern basins, whereas localized underestimation occurred in portions of the Midwest and western United States. Overall, Schaake96 showed the strongest low‐flow performance, while GrUB provided relatively small low‐flow errors and balanced overall performance using independently derived parameters without basin‐specific streamflow calibration. These results highlight substantial differences among Noah‐MP runoff and groundwater configurations and their representation of low‐flow processes.

articles.title: A neural code for generative speech production in human Wernicke’s area
articles.titleEn: A neural code for generative speech production in human Wernicke’s area
articles.abstract: Wernicke’s area in the posterior temporal lobe is classically defined by its role in speech comprehension, yet a paradox remains: Why does damage here also profoundly impair speech production? Using direct human brain recordings, cortical stimulation, and lesion analysis, we found that this region is not solely for perception. A discrete subzone within Wernicke’s area, the left posterior superior temporal gyrus (lpSTG), becomes active before speech, is causally necessary for speech production, and codes features of whole upcoming words rather than low-level acoustics or articulatory information. Its neural activity is distinct from the auditory-feedback responses nearby and can decode intended speech in people with paralysis. Thus, while Wernicke’s area is a key part of auditory cortex, it contains a dedicated subregion for speech generation.

articles.title: Methane outburst driven by magma–sediment interactions at Fentale Volcano detected by satellite
articles.titleEn: Methane outburst driven by magma–sediment interactions at Fentale Volcano detected by satellite
articles.abstract: Magmatic intrusions into sedimentary rocks can release carbon-based greenhouse gases, dominantly methane, and have been linked to rapid changes in past climate. However, modern volcanic systems typically emit very little methane, meaning that appropriate analogues are lacking. Here we report satellite measurements of an outburst of methane and carbon dioxide from a restless but non-erupting volcano in the East African Rift. Following a mega-dyke intrusion in 2025, Fentale Volcano (Ethiopia) released at least 38.2 ± 3.9 kt CH 4 over 3 months and at least 2.9 ± 1.0 MtCO 2 . The peak methane emission rate of 157 ± 41 t h −1 is comparable to major industrial blowouts and approximately four orders of magnitude higher than methane emission rates from other volcanic systems. The emissions coincided with localized ground subsidence and thermal anomalies within Fentale’s caldera. We propose that the intrusion disrupted an impermeable cap beneath which methane, derived from hydrocarbon-rich sediments, was trapped. This single outburst is small compared with annual emissions from natural and anthropogenic sources, but demonstrates an unrecognized source of episodic methane emissions, providing insight into greenhouse gas release from magmatic–sedimentary systems.

articles.title: Atmospheric organic nitrogen is a major nutrient source to global oceans
articles.titleEn: Atmospheric organic nitrogen is a major nutrient source to global oceans
articles.abstract: Atmospheric nitrogen (N) deposition is a critical nutrient source for marine ecosystems, but its organic nitrogen (ON) component remains poorly quantified. We measured ON in marine aerosols collected during 21 research cruises transecting multiple ocean basins and both hemispheric high latitudes. We used these observations to constrain and evaluate an atmospheric chemistry model with updated ON sources and sinks, enabling global mapping of ON deposition. The model estimated annual ON deposition to oceans at 12.8 (4.0 to 22.7) teragrams of nitrogen per year (Tg N year −1 ), contributing 27% (11 to 40%) of total N deposition. Marine emissions supply 3.9 (0.7 to 6.9) Tg N year −1 (30%) of deposited ON, while terrestrial sources contribute 8.9 (3.3 to 15.7) Tg N year −1 (70%). In N-limited regions such as the central Atlantic and Indonesian seas, ON accounts for ~50% of total N deposition.

articles.title: Widespread marine mammal and seabird reductions are unlikely to benefit salmon due to indirect ecosystem effects
articles.titleEn: Widespread marine mammal and seabird reductions are unlikely to benefit salmon due to indirect ecosystem effects
articles.abstract: Pacific salmon are depleted due to anthropogenic impacts, and populations have failed to recover despite management interventions. Predation on salmon by pinnipeds and seabirds has been suggested as a barrier to recovery, leading to calls for predator culls by some. However, no studies have evaluated the whole-ecosystem impact of removing these predators nor estimated the direct and indirect effects of these culls on salmon. We use an end-to-end ecosystem model to assess the efficacy of widespread culls in marine environments. We find that culls are unlikely to benefit salmon due to the indirect food web effects of predator reduction and the low biomass of top predator groups. Instead, more abundant fish predators, northward-expanding competitors, and temperature-sensitive prey have larger effects on salmon in the ocean.

articles.title: The scientific record is never finished
articles.titleEn: The scientific record is never finished
articles.abstract: The scholarly scientific record has always been a work in progress. From the earliest days of scientific publishing, new findings would come along that changed the way earlier findings are understood. When research journals were published only in print, occasional errors would be reported by the authors or found by others, and papers would be retracted or corrected. When publishing became digital, many more people could quickly access and scrutinize data and images for accuracy. Now, in the age of artificial intelligence (AI), it is possible for machines to do these examinations more expeditiously and at a larger scale. All of this has added an important new layer to the publishing process and put more responsibility on authors, who must update their work if new issues arise. In response to this need, Science is improving the ways in which it will flag and notate papers that require adjustment or where changes are under consideration. Our Editorial Policies now reflect these updates.

articles.title: A thalamo-amygdalar circuit drives female vulnerability to chronic pain after early-life stress
articles.titleEn: A thalamo-amygdalar circuit drives female vulnerability to chronic pain after early-life stress
articles.abstract: Childhood adversity increases the risk of chronic pain and anxiety later in life, particularly in women, yet the neural mechanisms linking early-life stress to adult vulnerability remain elusive. Here, we show that social isolation and nerve injury interact to amplify activity-dependent synaptic gain and anticipatory recruitment of the paraventricular thalamus-to–central amygdala pathway in female, but not male, mice. This female-specific circuit sensitization enhances mechanical hypersensitivity and avoidance behaviors in adulthood. Chemogenetic pathway inhibition selectively rescued these behaviors when stress and injury co-occurred, whereas sustained and phasic pathway activation triggered mechanical hypersensitivity and avoidance, respectively. Together, these findings uncovered a latent thalamo-amygdalar synaptic gain state that is unmasked by a subsequent injury and transforms early-life stress into female-specific vulnerability to chronic pain and anxiety-like avoidance.

articles.title: Quaternary carbon–guided carbocation cascade rearrangement to enantioenriched polycycles
articles.titleEn: Quaternary carbon–guided carbocation cascade rearrangement to enantioenriched polycycles
articles.abstract: Polycyclic frameworks are prevalent in natural products and bioactive molecules, yet their efficient enantioselective synthesis remains a longstanding challenge. Carbocation cascade cyclization is a textbook reaction that has transformed the synthesis of fused polycycles, but extending this strategy to bridged architectures requires precise control over highly reactive carbocation intermediates while overcoming the intrinsic energetic barrier of transannular cyclization. Herein, we report a quaternary-carbon-guided carbocation cascade rearrangement platform that enables enantioselective and divergent assembly of complex polycyclic architectures from readily available substrates. An enantioenriched quaternary center, installed via transition-metal-catalyzed allylation, serves as a temporary structural linchpin in an acid-triggered cationic cascade rearrangement process, forming multiple bonds and chiral centers in a single step. In combination with pre-embedded quaternary centers, this strategy provides bicyclic and bridged polycyclic frameworks bearing multiple stereocenters with high enantioselectivity.

articles.title: Using a Gaussian process emulator to approximate short-term climate response patterns to greenhouse gas and aerosol forcings
articles.titleEn: Using a Gaussian process emulator to approximate short-term climate response patterns to greenhouse gas and aerosol forcings
articles.abstract: We present a Gaussian process emulator for estimating fast surface temperature response patterns to a range of different climate forcing agents, including both long-lived greenhouse gases and short-lived pollutants such as aerosols. This emulator is trained on simulations driven by perturbations to emissions (for short-lived pollutants) and concentrations (for long-lived greenhouse gases) using a full-complexity global climate model and predicts the response in the first five years after the forcing, at a small fraction of the computational cost. We outline the emulator design, including the choice of pollutant perturbations and the input space covered by the training data. We show that the emulator performs well in most regions of the chosen input space, except under very large aerosol perturbations. A global sensitivity analysis is carried out to characterize and understand emission-response relationships for each pollutant. We find similar large-scale patterns of sensitivity to aerosol pollutants released in different regions. Our work demonstrates the potential for rapid climate change projections subject to various climate forcing agents, focusing on the short-term response. articles.title: Climate suitability of East Asian mangroves for nature-based solutions is limited by climate extremes
articles.titleEn: Climate suitability of East Asian mangroves for nature-based solutions is limited by climate extremes
articles.abstract: Mangroves represent distinctive coastal ecosystems that offer ecological benefits, notably through their high carbon sequestration rates. However, their resilience to extreme climate events remains uncertain. Here, we investigated the response of mangroves in East Asia to climate variability by employing the remote-sensing derived Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) as a proxy for canopy greenness. A bootstrapping-based statistical framework was applied to identify vegetation responses associated with extreme climate events and quantify lagged climatic effects. We found East Asian mangrove NDVI variability was strongly influenced by preceding winter temperature and seasonal solar radiation, with distinct lagged responses on seasonal time scales across latitudinal zones. These findings were extrapolated to future projections by the Earth system modelling to assess future climate suitability for existing mangroves and for areas of potential thermal suitability in East Asia, particularly China, South Korea and Japan. While shifts in wintertime isotherms suggest a northward shift in the thermal range of mangroves under global warming, low solar radiation events associated with aerosol emissions under the high-emission SSP3-7.0 scenario could constrain future climatic suitability for mangroves. This study highlights that both temperature-driven opportunities and solar radiation constraints should be integrated into practical planning for future conservation, restoration, and migration as nature-based climate solutions.

articles.title: The SOLCHECK project: An investigation into the imprints of solar variability across multiple timescales
articles.titleEn: The SOLCHECK project: An investigation into the imprints of solar variability across multiple timescales
articles.abstract: The project Solar Contribution to Climate Change on Decadal to Centennial Timescales (SOLCHECK) investigated the influence of solar variability on the atmosphere from the pre-industrial era to the present and future. Variations in solar output ranging from weeks to millennia leave distinct imprints on the climate system. Their assessment is, however, challenging because of limited observations, incomplete representation of feedback processes in climate models, and computational constraints. Using a large ensemble of simulations with advanced chemistry–climate models and realistic solar forcing, SOLCHECK aimed to reduce uncertainties in atmospheric solar imprints and to assess the sensitivity of the atmospheric response across timescales and climate states. One key result is that although the initial radiative and chemical responses to the 11-year solar cycle are consistent across models in the upper tropical stratosphere, a robust assessment of tropospheric and surface solar signatures in northern winter is limited due to the variable impact of the stratospheric polar vortex. SOLCHECK also shows that the climate system responds differently to solar forcing under past, present, and future conditions, with stronger responses in the tropical upper troposphere and Arctic as anthropogenic warming progresses. Moreover, extreme solar storms may substantially reduce stratospheric ozone up to a year, with increases in skin-damaging UV of a few percent at northern subtropical and mid-latitudes in spring/summer.

articles.title: Spatial patterns in indirect effects of human activity on climate, land, and water: comparing top-down and bottom-up clustering approaches
articles.titleEn: Spatial patterns in indirect effects of human activity on climate, land, and water: comparing top-down and bottom-up clustering approaches
articles.abstract: In order to assess the full systemic impact of anthropogenic pressures on climate and land, it is crucial to account for indirect impacts mediated by bio-geophysical processes. These impacts typically display a high spatial heterogeneity. In this study, we systematically compare the ability of top-down and bottom-up clustering approaches to capture the spatial patterns in indirect effects on climate, land, and water. Effect sizes are estimated based on simulations conducted with an offline global spatial vegetation model. Following a top-down approach, we map the resulting global pattern on common natural partitions of the Earth. Cluster validity indices reveal a close alignment between the indirect impacts of land use change on climate and an Earth partition into biomes. In contrast, the indirect impacts of climate- and land use change on surface water runoff are best captured by the Köppen-Geiger climate zones. Adopting a bottom-up approach, we employ multivariate spatially constrained clustering to derive an integrative global partition. Several patches of tropical rainforest on the Indomalayan islands as well as large areas of warm grasslands in Australia are identified as high-impact clusters. The results of this study should be considered illustrative as they are based on only one dynamical vegetation model. Nevertheless, they emphasize the local nature of indirect impacts and elucidate the potential and limitations of both top-down and bottom-up spatial aggregation.

articles.title: Ground-truthing the application of compound-specific stable isotopes of amino acids to planktic foraminifera tests from Santa Barbara Basin
articles.titleEn: Ground-truthing the application of compound-specific stable isotopes of amino acids to planktic foraminifera tests from Santa Barbara Basin
articles.abstract: Planktic foraminifera form shells that are preserved in ocean sediments and are used in a variety of paleoproxy and biostratigraphic applications. However, species-specific ecology can complicate the interpretation of planktic foraminifera-based proxies, and limited options exist for examining the ecology of extinct species. Here we apply test-bound compound-specific stable isotopes of amino acids (CSI-AA) to examine the trophic ecology of extant planktic foraminifera. We measure CSI-AA in planktic foraminifera shells collected in sediment traps from the Santa Barbara Basin, CA, specifically the three most abundant species in this region: Globigerina bulloides , Neogloboquadrina incompta , and Turborotalita quinqueloba . The nitrogen CSI-AA of all three species suggest that planktic foraminifera have metazoan-like metabolisms, and that trophic position estimates using CSI-AA are appropriate for planktic foraminifera. All three species had trophic positions near 2 (primary consumer), with no evidence for mixotrophy or photosymbionts. Carbon CSI-AA, in combination with a Bayesian stable isotope mixing model, indicates that the three species occupied separate niches based on diet. Globigerina bulloides fed opportunistically on all groups of phytoplankton available in Santa Barbara Basin, adjusting its diet with seasonal changes in phytoplankton assemblage. Turborotalita quinqueloba specialized in diatoms but consumed some heterotrophic bacteria and cyanobacteria. Neogloboquadrina incompta consumed primarily heterotrophic bacteria and some dinoflagellates. Our results align with the current understanding of each species' ecology while further defining their niches. Our findings suggest that CSI-AA is a promising tool for understanding the trophic ecology of planktic foraminifera, and we make recommendations for future applications of CSI-AA to fossil specimens.

articles.title: Acidification in coastal waters of Adélie Land, Antarctica (1985–2025)
articles.titleEn: Acidification in coastal waters of Adélie Land, Antarctica (1985–2025)
articles.abstract: Ocean acidification is expected to be particularly severe in Antarctic continental shelves due to enhanced anthropogenic carbon uptake in cold waters in response to rising atmospheric CO 2 , sea-ice retreat, freshening and climate-change feedbacks. Models suggest that undersaturated conditions with respect to aragonite (Ω ar ), a major form of calcium carbonate formed by marine species, could be reached as soon as 2052 for austral winter. Here we present new ocean carbonate system observations from cruises conducted since 2010 in the Adélie Land coastal region in East Antarctica, along with data from a BCG-Argo float and results from a neural network model for the period 1985–2025. The region is a permanent CO 2 sink which was most pronounced since 2006. The CO 2 sink leads to an increase of surface water total CO 2 concentrations ( C T ) (+0.44 ± 0.01 µmolkg-1yr-1) and to a decrease of pH (−0.013 per decade) and Ω ar (−0.035 per decade) for the winter season. The lowest surface Ω ar of 1.2 was observed in winter 2024 from the float data, a critical limit for some marine species such as pteropods. A projection of the C T concentrations in the future, based on observed anthropogenic CO 2 concentrations and emissions scenarios, suggests that aragonite saturation state (Ω ar = 1) will occur in surface waters as soon as 2055 in the Adélie Land region, which is part of a larger area of East Antarctica proposed as a Marine Protected Area by the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources since the early 2010s.

articles.title: Retreating glaciers and snow cover are amplifying summer droughts in the upper Adige River Basin (Italy)
articles.titleEn: Retreating glaciers and snow cover are amplifying summer droughts in the upper Adige River Basin (Italy)
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: Snow and glacier meltwater play a critical role in sustaining summer streamflow in mountains and downstream regions. Yet, understanding glaciers' contributions to buffer river streamflow during droughts remains limited and poses major barriers to improve present and future water management within the context of climate change. This study evaluates the contribution of glacier melt to summer flows and its role in mitigating hydrological droughts in the upper Adige River basin (Italy). We developed and implemented a new dynamic glacier module into the ICHYMOD-TOPMELT hydrological model, annually updating glacier area and improving the quantification of meltwater contributions under progressive glacier retreat (from 111 km 2 in 1997 to 79 km 2 in 2017). The hydrological model exhibited robust performance (KGE = 0.89 for 1997–2022 for the whole upper Adige River basin at the Bronzolo closing station; 0.88 in summers) capturing observed glacier area, mass balance, and seasonal melt trends. Results show that glacier melt in the upper Adige River basin contributed an average of 4.5 % to total summer streamflow during 1997–2022, with significant spatial variability, reaching 30 % in glacierized subbasins. During the severe droughts of 2003, 2005 and 2022, glacier melt contributions ranged between 4 % and 12 % at the upper Adige closing section. In 2003, high temperature and limited Snow Water Equivalent (SWE) led to glacier melt accounting for 11.67 % of summer flows. By contrast, the significant runoff deficit in 2005 was driven by colder temperatures, which reduced glacier melt contributions to 4.85 %, combined with low SWE conditions. In 2022, the combination of low precipitation, low snow cover and high temperature drove glacier melt. In contrast to the 2003 drought, reduced glacier areas led to lower absolute contributions (8.17 %). Our findings reveal that despite the increased melt rates in recent warm years, retreating glacier areas have reduced their absolute buffering effect. Glacier retreat is weakening the contribution of glaciers to summer flows, increasing the upper Adige River basin's dependence on precipitation and snowmelt, the latter of which is also showing a decreasing trend. For these reasons, accounting for dynamic glacier and snow changes is essential to improve future drought projections and inform adaptive water management in glacier-fed basins within the context of climate and anthropogenic changes.

articles.title: Evidence for p-wave magnetism in electronic band structure of metallic EuSi
articles.titleEn: Evidence for p-wave magnetism in electronic band structure of metallic EuSi
articles.abstract: One active frontier of quantum-matter research is the realization of p -wave symmetry-breaking phases in fermionic systems, long exemplified by the A phase of superfluid helium-3 (refs. 1–3 ). Achieving p -wave superconductivity 4 and its magnetic analogue 5 —characterized by a time-reversal-symmetric, p -wave spin-polarized Fermi surface—remains a grand challenge 6,7 . Despite recent progress in identifying candidate p -wave magnets 5,7–10 , spin-resolved spectroscopic evidence for their electronic structures remains limited. Here we report angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) and spin-ARPES evidence for p -wave magnetism in the near-Fermi-level electronic structure of stoichiometric metallic EuSi, supported by symmetry analysis, first-principles calculations and neutron scattering. Neutron diffraction reveals a chiral spiral phase between 33.4 K and 62 K that fulfils archetypal p -wave magnetism criteria: it preserves the combined symmetry of time reversal and lattice translation, while breaking inversion symmetry. Spin-integrated ARPES reveals a pronounced magnetism-driven reconstruction of the electronic structure, with energy separations exceeding 100 meV, and spin-ARPES resolves S y polarization in near-Fermi-level spectral features. The extracted S y exhibits a sign-changing modulation across successive magnetic Brillouin zones and is suppressed near the nodal regions, consistent with the predicted p -wave spin texture and unfolded spin-polarization calculations. Magnetic force microscopy and micro-ARPES further reveal approximately 10-μm chiral magnetic domains. These results identify EuSi as a stoichiometric metallic platform for investigating p -wave magnetism in electronic band structures and spin-symmetry-based functionalities in spintronics 10 , topological matter 7 , superconductivity 11 and beyond.

articles.title: Hydromorphodynamic Impacts Extend Beyond the Recirculation Zone of a Spur Dike on a Mobile Bed
articles.titleEn: Hydromorphodynamic Impacts Extend Beyond the Recirculation Zone of a Spur Dike on a Mobile Bed
articles.abstract: Spur dikes generate a recirculation zone, and reattachment length is used to estimate hydraulic effects and guide structure spacing. Fixed‐bed studies of non‐submerged, impermeable spur dikes commonly report primary recirculation lengths on the order of 10 dike lengths, but direct measurements over deformed mobile beds remain sparse. We test whether the end of the recirculation region also marks the end of the downstream flow and bed response. We analyze a 32‐day clear‐water mobile‐bed flume experiment with post‐run three‐component velocity measurements and a final bed survey. Across two elevations and two criteria, estimates of the primary reverse‐flow extent span 1.00–2.68 dike lengths. At the same measured locations in each included section, the difference from the upstream velocity field reached a local minimum at eight dike lengths, then increased, with later values above the comparison level through 16 dike lengths. The farther downstream reach contained an oblique depositional macroform and about 96% of the mapped deposition. At the final velocity section, 20 dike lengths downstream, the streamwise momentum‐flux centroid on the common coordinates was displaced toward the structure side, having reversed between 12 and 16 dike lengths, while the lower part of the flow still showed momentum deficit, elevated turbulence, and secondary circulation. Structure‐side bed deformation extended to the survey limit at 24 dike lengths. In this experiment, the primary recirculation region was therefore short relative to the longer reach of altered flow and bed topography. Reattachment length alone did not describe the full downstream response of the mobile‐bed channel.

articles.title: Exploring Climatic, Soil, and Topographic Controls on Continental Patterns in Suspended Sediment Concentration
articles.titleEn: Exploring Climatic, Soil, and Topographic Controls on Continental Patterns in Suspended Sediment Concentration
articles.abstract: High concentrations of suspended sediment (SSC) in a river can represent a critical water quality concern, reduce the storage capacity of reservoirs, and impact aquatic habitat. Within a river, SSC can be conceptualized as a function of reach‐scale hydraulics translating discharge into shear stress and watershed processes that determine the types and quantities of sediment supplied to the river. To explore watershed controls on sediment supply, we utilized SSC data from 1,007 US Geological Survey gages across the continental United States (CONUS). We find that the geometric mean (GM) SSC spans over five orders of magnitude with spatial correlations across CONUS. Here we utilize publicly available geospatial data sets (topography, soils, and climate) to explore potential drivers of the continental pattern of GM SSC. We reduced 345 candidate geospatial variables (attributes and their summary statistics) to eight variables. We find that these geospatial variables provide few robust explanatory univariate trends across the observed variation in GM SSC. A five‐fold cross‐validated multiple nonlinear regression reveals that the geospatial pattern in GM SSC is most strongly associated with climate, topographic, and soil properties; however, the substantial variability in GM SSC prevents confident CONUS‐wide predictions. Exploration of the outlier values reveals that dams, arid and actively meandering river dynamics are poorly captured within existing geospatial data sets. Understanding SSC dependence on watershed properties remains an important pathway for linking watershed processes and management strategies to fine‐grained transport dynamics given uncertain future hydroclimatic and environmental change.

articles.title: Observation‐Anchored Machine Learning for Baseflow Estimation in India
articles.titleEn: Observation‐Anchored Machine Learning for Baseflow Estimation in India
articles.abstract: Baseflow is critical for maintaining river flows, supporting ecosystems, and meeting water demands during dry periods. Yet, large‐scale estimation of baseflow remains challenging due to the lack of direct observations. Here, we present HyGBR‐Baseflow, a machine learning framework that estimates baseflow by anchoring the learning to reference points (RPs) and read directly from streamflow recession. The framework uses four graphical and five digital filter methods as predictors, together with hydrometeorological variables. To address the scarcity of reliable training data during monsoon season, our framework uses pseudo‐reference points (PRPs), derived from the mean baseflow of the three best‐performing baseflow separation methods and assigns reduced sample weights (0.2–0.5) compared to true RPs. We applied HyGBR‐Baseflow to 227 stations across 18 major Indian River basins for 1961–2021 and evaluated its performance using Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency, Kling–Gupta Efficiency, refined index of agreement, and R 2 . Overall, the HyGBR‐Baseflow framework consistently outperformed individual baseflow separation methods, with the largest improvements during the monsoon season across diverse hydrological regimes. The baseflow trend analysis showed pronounced declines in several catchments. Even the Ganga and Brahmaputra basins, which comprise catchments where baseflow contributes more than 70% of the total streamflow at most stations, showed declining baseflow trends. Additionally, the long‐term baseflow index indicated higher baseflow contributions in humid catchments compared to semi‐arid and dry sub‐humid regions. The HyGBR‐Baseflow provides a scalable, accurate, and observation‐anchored nonlinear reconciliation framework for baseflow estimation that can support groundwater–surface water interaction studies, water resources planning, drought monitoring, and climate change impact assessments across India.

To address the scarcity of reliable training data during monsoon season, our framework uses pseudo‐reference points (PRPs), derived from the mean baseflow of the three best‐performing baseflow separation methods and assigns reduced sample weights (0.2–0.5) compared to true RPs. Overall, the HyGBR‐Baseflow framework consistently outperformed individual baseflow separation methods, with the largest improvements during the monsoon season across diverse hydrological regimes. The baseflow trend analysis showed pronounced declines in several catchments. Even the Ganga and Brahmaputra basins, which comprise catchments where baseflow contributes more than 70% of the total streamflow at most stations, showed declining baseflow trends. Additionally, the long‐term baseflow index indicated higher baseflow contributions in humid catchments compared to semi‐arid and dry sub‐humid regions. The HyGBR‐Baseflow provides a scalable, accurate, and observation‐anchored nonlinear reconciliation framework for baseflow estimation that can support groundwater–surface water interaction studies, water resources planning, drought monitoring, and climate change impact assessments across India.

articles.title: Identifying Dominant Environmental Predictors of Coastal Shallow Groundwater Levels Across Diel to Seasonal Time Scales
articles.titleEn: Identifying Dominant Environmental Predictors of Coastal Shallow Groundwater Levels Across Diel to Seasonal Time Scales
articles.abstract: Coastal zone, especially mega‐deltas are densely populated and socioeconomically important, where shallow groundwater responds to interacting terrestrial, marine, atmospheric and engineered influences across multiple time scales, contributing to uncertainty in groundwater prediction. Here, we utilized a multiscale information‐theoretic diagnostic framework to analyze groundwater‐level (GWL) dynamics in the Yellow River Delta and to identifying dominant environmental predictors of coastal shallow groundwater levels across diel to seasonal time scales. Results indicate that: (a) the seasonal component dominates GWL variability, accounting for 73% of total variance. Air temperature ( T ) serves as the primary predictor at sites closer to the coastline, whereas precipitation ( P ) dominates at sites farther inland. Seasonal GWL is asynchronous with T and P, with offsets of 27 ± 23 and 13 days, respectively. (b) the multiday component accounts for 25% of total variance; here, evaporative demand drives recession dynamics, while P induces episodic recharge pulses (lag: 1.1 ± 0.25 days). (c) the diel component (2% of variance) exhibits regular diel cycles. P outperforms potential evapotranspiration (PET) as the dominant predictor, suggesting that rapid infiltration events generate intense high‐frequency hydraulic signals that outweigh regular diel evapotranspiration oscillations in information content. Near tidal channels, tides dominate, with GWL lagging tidal stage by 4 hr. By explicitly resolving time‐scale dependence, asynchrony, and nonlinearity, this study advances the understanding of coastal shallow GWL dynamics and provides a basis for GWL prediction, model development, and coastal groundwater management.

articles.title: Assessing the contribution of extratropical cyclones to river floods that caused property damage in Quebec, Canada
articles.titleEn: Assessing the contribution of extratropical cyclones to river floods that caused property damage in Quebec, Canada
articles.abstract: In the past few decades, the province of Quebec in eastern Canada has experienced widespread and costly flood events, yet the contribution of extratropical cyclones to these floods remains unquantified. This paper presents a methodology for analysing the contribution of extratropical cyclones (ETCs) to 498 fluvial floods that occurred in watersheds in southern Quebec, Canada, between 1991 and 2020, and highlights key characteristics shared by the 200 flood ETCs (storms that contributed to flooding) identified in the study. This analysis combined reconstituted river outputs, government financial aid claims following flooding, ETC tracks, and precipitation data to identify flood events and their relevant ETCs. ETC contribution was defined as the percentage of rainfall during a search window surrounding each flood event that was associated with the relevant ETCs. Most of these floods occurred in the spring (74.7 %). The majority (72.7 %) of flood events had a high (50 %–75 %) to very high (>75 %) ETC contribution, and only 2.6 % of events (mostly occurring in summer) had a negligible ( Baseline Southern Quebec domain , N =6027). Flood ETCs also spent on average 18.2 h more in the domain and generally tracked over southern Quebec as opposed to over the Atlantic Ocean along the east coast of North America or over northern Quebec like non-flood ETCs. The percentages of financial aid claims allotted to flood ETCs were highly variable. Just five of the 200 flood ETCs were associated with 51.0 % of all financial aid claims filed during the 30-year period, indicating that a high to very high ETC contribution rarely resulted in widespread flooding. The method developed in this study could be applied to other regions or types of storms analysed (e.g. tropical cyclones and mesoscale convective systems) to further our understanding of the atmospheric causes of flooding in northeastern North America.

articles.title: Process diagnostics of snowmelt runoff in global hydrological and land surface models – Part 2: Are more complex models better?
articles.titleEn: Process diagnostics of snowmelt runoff in global hydrological and land surface models – Part 2: Are more complex models better?
articles.abstract: The added value of increased process complexity has long been a central yet unresolved question in hydrological modeling, particularly for snowmelt runoff (SMR), where multiple physical processes interact in complex ways. We then systematically revisit the important linkage between model complexity and model performance in three distinct SMR characteristics, i.e., total runoff ( Q sum ), peak flow ( Q max ), and centroid timing (CTQ) of runoff in the snowmelt period. Further, we assess how the basin complexity (as delineated by 1455 snow-dominated basins), forcing difference and calibration status can modulate this linkage. Interestingly, we find a positive correlation between snow-process complexity and model performance for CTQ ( r =0.32). articles.title: Benefits of multi-target and self-supervised LSTM models for water quantity and quality
articles.titleEn: Benefits of multi-target and self-supervised LSTM models for water quantity and quality
articles.abstract: Deep learning has become a standard tool for streamflow modelling, but its application to water quality remains challenging due to sparse, irregular, and noisy in-situ observations. Yet, water-quality variables are tightly linked to discharge and to each other through shared hydrological and biogeochemical controls, suggesting that jointly modelling water quantity and quality may help compensate for limited data availability. In this study, we compare single-target, multi-target, and self-supervised LSTM models for the joint simulation of discharge and six water-quality variables (NO 3 -N, PO 4 -P, DO, DOC, EC, and WT) across 408 German catchments. Our results highlight that extending the baseline LSTM from single-target discharge prediction to jointly predicting discharge and all six water-quality variables does not substantially degrade discharge performance (across all baseline configurations, median KGE ′ = 0.84–0.87) and yields median KGE ′ values between 0.40 (PO 4 -P) and 0.95 (WT) for the water-quality targets. Interestingly, learning discharge as a co-target matches or exceeds the performance of using observed discharge as an additional input for five of the six water-quality variables, with the clearest gain for DOC (ΔKGE ′ = +0.05). This indicates that jointly learning water quantity and quality can be more effective than using discharge as a predictor. A variable-averaged loss function is key to balance the strongly uneven observation densities of discharge and water-quality variables. Building on this multi-target framework, we further explore whether an alternative training strategy based on self-supervised learning can better exploit the incomplete and heterogeneous nature of environmental observations. Our evaluation reveals that the self-supervised LSTM yields a level of predictive skill comparable to the multi-target supervised baseline LSTM under inference conditions restricted to meteorological drivers and when contextual water-quality data is provided. Thus, while matching the baseline's skill, the self-supervised LSTM gains versatility, as a single model can be applied to many different combinations of available input data without retraining. Besides showcasing the strong performance of LSTMs in water-quality simulations with sparse and irregular data, our results demonstrate that multi-target learning provides an effective framework for coupled water quantity–quality modelling, while self-supervised learning offers additional flexibility for exploiting incomplete and heterogeneous environmental observations.

articles.title: Verification of coastal enhanced weathering by tracking the dissolution of alkaline minerals: theory and laboratory tests with olivine
articles.titleEn: Verification of coastal enhanced weathering by tracking the dissolution of alkaline minerals: theory and laboratory tests with olivine
articles.abstract: Coastal Enhanced Weathering (CEW) is a marine Carbon Dioxide Removal (CDR) method that adds ground alkaline minerals to shallow regions of the ocean in order to increase seawater alkalinity, i.e. its capacity for storing atmospheric CO 2 as bicarbonate. While CEW is promising with regard to cost and scalability, it is an uncontained, “open-system” style of CDR, and presents significant challenges to effective measurement, reporting, and verification (MRV) of the process. In particular, quantifying how much alkalinity is released from an added amount of mineral is challenging as the minerals dissolve and release alkalinity over wide spatial and long temporal scales. Such quantification is further complicated by the fact that dissolved alkalinity is rapidly diluted below detectable concentrations. Here, we propose an approach to quantify alkalinity formation that relies on solid sediment tracers to track mineral grains underwater and measure how much they have dissolved over time. In theory, the amount of dissolution at any given point in time is proportional to the amount of alkalinity released. Thus, the approach aims to overcome the near impossible detection of alkalinity accumulation in the dissolved phase by tracking the loss of alkaline material in the solid phase. We describe a test of the fundamental aspects of this method including the measurement of the mineral and tracer content of a sediment sample, and the extent to which those measurements correlate with changes in seawater chemistry. While the specific tracer used in this experiment proved unsuitable for this method, we found that olivine dissolution significantly increased alkalinity in seawater compared to control incubators. X-Ray Diffraction (XRD) was able to quantify the change in the olivine in the sediment (albeit with large relative errors) and automated particle counting methods were able to enumerate tracer particles when illuminated under UV-A light. These results are insufficient to fully substantiate this method, but rather serve as an illustration of, and proof-of-principle of, a new approach to measure alkalinity addition to the ocean resulting from CEW deployments. By publishing these findings as a LESSONS (Limitations, Errors, Surprises, Shortcomings, Opportunities for New Science) Report we aim to present and introduce a promising opportunity for new science that we hope will spur a thorough and robust investigation of this method in the broader research community.

articles.title: Global Potential of Agrivoltaics: Agriculture‐First and Radiation‐Limited Analysis
articles.titleEn: Global Potential of Agrivoltaics: Agriculture‐First and Radiation‐Limited Analysis
articles.abstract: With rising global food and energy demand, agrivoltaics offer a viable solution for co‐producing crops and solar electricity on shared land. Despite extensive field‐scale design and optimization studies, a large‐scale, crop‐specific assessment constrained by light availability is still missing. Here, we introduce a radiation‐limited framework that uses growing‐season daily light integral (DLI) to set minimum light budgets for wheat, maize, rice, and soybean, and the agrivoltaics light utilization ratio (ALUR) metric to quantify the surplus light available for photovoltaic (PV) electricity generation. This enables a global first‐order assessment of light availability revealing regional potentials and constraints to agrivoltaic adoption. Four agrivoltaic scenarios were explored by varying the light reserved for the crop: (a) literature‐based crop light targets (SC T,crop ), (b) empirical reference values representing the growing‐season light received across the global distribution of each crop (SC R,crop ), (c) a low reserve favoring electricity generation (SC 20 ; 20 mol m −2 day −1 ), and (d) a conservative reserve favoring food security (SC 40 ; 40 mol m −2 day −1 ). Even under the conservative scenario SC 40 , the total estimated mean global electricity‐generation potential is 109 PWh yr −1 (95% uncertainty interval: 39–190 PWh yr −1 ). The estimated radiation‐based potential is sensitive to the crop‐specific DLI allocation, particularly in India and China, but remains substantial across the United States, Brazil, Argentina, Iran, and Pakistan. These findings suggest that while agrivoltaics are not a “one‐size‐fits‐all” solution, their strategic application can mitigate the land‐use conflict between energy and food production.

articles.title: Simulating Cloud‐Driven Turbulence in Stratocumulus Cloud Systems Over Sea Ice in Weather‐Scale Models
articles.titleEn: Simulating Cloud‐Driven Turbulence in Stratocumulus Cloud Systems Over Sea Ice in Weather‐Scale Models
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: Stratocumulus cloud systems play a fundamental role in the climate system due to their impact on the surface radiation budget and boundary layer structure. One of the challenges in modeling these cloud systems is how to represent sub‐grid processes. This study is focused on evaluating and improving the representation of cloud‐driven sub‐grid turbulence in weather‐scale models over sea ice, where stratocumulus clouds decoupled from surface sources of heat and moisture frequently occur. The planetary boundary layer scheme used in the current NOAA Global Forecast System (GFS) to simulate cloud‐driven turbulence is evaluated in nested limited area simulations of a stratocumulus cloud system in the western Arctic and then tested in a single column model (SCM) using a central Arctic case from the Multidisciplinary drifting Observatory for the Study of Arctic Climate expedition. The inner cloud‐resolving nest is used to evaluate coarser nests. The default configuration of this boundary layer scheme uses a mass flux formulation based on a parameterization of surface‐forced thermal plumes to simulate top‐down mixing in stratocumulus systems forced by cloud‐top radiative cooling. It is demonstrated that when a mixed layer model formulation of sub‐grid cloud‐driven turbulence is used instead of the mass flux scheme, it can reproduce the variability of the cloud‐resolving nest while the mass flux formulation produces significant biases in sub‐grid energy and water fluxes, which produce compensating biases in microphysics. This new formulation for sub‐grid cloud‐driven turbulence is shown to have similar results in an SCM run with a GFS prototype physics suite.

articles.title: Flat-band-induced integer doping and phase transition in monolayer graphene
articles.titleEn: Flat-band-induced integer doping and phase transition in monolayer graphene
articles.abstract: van der Waals heterostructures are stabilized by a delicate balance between van der Waals, elastic and Coulomb energies 1–4 . Because the interfaces are not covalently bonded, the constituent crystals can slide, rotate and reconstruct, resulting in several possible competing structural phases 2,5,6 . However, controlled tuning of this balance, and hence dynamical control over the stacking, has yet to be achieved. Here we report a dynamical heterostructure in which monolayer graphene is doubly aligned to bulk hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) and monolayer hexagonal boron nitride (mhBN) on either side. In such a system, a global structural phase transition, manifested as a change of crystalline symmetry observed by scanning tunnelling microscopy, could be induced by gating, magnetic field or temperature. This structural transition is accompanied by an exotic electronic transition: the doping of graphene switches between discrete levels, corresponding to an exact integer number of electrons or holes per moiré plaquette. We attribute this integer doping to charge trapping in localized, strain-induced pseudo-Landau levels (flat bands in reciprocal space 7–12 ), produced by moiré reconstruction (strongly enhanced by the mhBN). Electrical control of coupled structural and electronic phase transitions provides a route to engineering strain-induced flat bands and strain–Coulomb correlations in van der Waals heterostructures.

articles.title: Ferroptosis in cancer cells triggers PGE2 production for tumour immune escape
articles.titleEn: Ferroptosis in cancer cells triggers PGE2 production for tumour immune escape
articles.abstract: Ferroptosis, a form of cell death induced by overwhelming membrane lipid peroxidation, is a vulnerability of many cancers, including cancers resistant to current molecular and immune-based therapies 1–7 . Triggering of ferroptosis therefore provides an opportunity to achieve elimination of difficult-to-treat cancers 1–4,8,9 . Studies in mouse cancer models have demonstrated that anticancer immunity, mediated by dendritic cells (DCs) and CD8 + T cells, is essential for effective tumour eradication by ferroptosis-inducing strategies 10–13 . However, ferroptotic cells limit this response 8–10,14 , resulting in immune escape and tumour growth through mechanisms that remain unclear. Here we demonstrate that ferroptotic cancer cells activate a molecular program resulting in aberrant production of prostaglandin E 2 (PGE 2 ), which limits the stimulation of anticancer CD8 + T cell responses by type 1 conventional DCs (cDC1s), thereby promoting immune escape. In ferroptotic cancer cells, lipid peroxidation-mediated membrane permeabilization enables Ca 2+ influx, which activates p38 MAPK signalling and thereby drives PGE 2 production. This signalling axis is uncoupled from cancer cell death and can be targeted to selectively interfere with immune-inhibitory PGE 2 production while preserving ferroptotic cancer cell elimination. In the context of cancer cell ferroptosis, ablation of PGE 2 production or disrupting PGE 2 signalling restores cDC1-mediated anticancer CD8 + T cell responses and leads to effective tumour elimination. Our findings identify a key mechanism that limits antitumour immunity and prevents tumour elimination upon ferroptosis induction in cancer cells, which could be exploited for cancer therapy.

articles.title: Injury-induced signalling coordinates immunity and cannibalism in locusts
articles.titleEn: Injury-induced signalling coordinates immunity and cannibalism in locusts
articles.abstract: Cannibalism, the consumption of conspecifics, is widespread across the animal kingdom and can profoundly influence individual fitness and population dynamics 1,2 . Although the ecological and social conditions that favour cannibalism have been well documented 2 , the molecular signals that trigger cannibalistic attacks have remained poorly understood. Here we show that in Locusta migratoria , guaiacol, a volatile compound with augmented release after injury, attracts gregarious nymphs and induces cannibalistic behaviour. Guaiacol is detected by olfactory receptors LmOR36 and LmOR34, and disruption of either receptor abolishes attraction, thereby impairing induction of cannibalism. Guaiacol is synthesized by haemolymph symbiont Enterobacter hormaechei . articles.title: Analogue simulation of massive relativistic quantum fields in 2 + 1 dimensions
articles.titleEn: Analogue simulation of massive relativistic quantum fields in 2 + 1 dimensions
articles.abstract: Quantum field theories provide fundamental models of complex interacting systems 1–3 , from high-energy physics and cosmology to condensed matter. However, solving these models in non-perturbative and dynamical regimes is often challenging, particularly in more than one spatial dimension. Analogue simulation using tunable synthetic quantum systems can both verify existing theoretical predictions and lead to physical insights. Here we realize analogue simulation of massive relativistic quantum fields in 2 + 1 dimensions (two spatial dimensions and time), using two coherently coupled spin components 4,5 in a uniform two-dimensional atomic Bose–Einstein condensate 6,7 . Specifically, we encode the paradigmatic sine-Gordon model 8,9 in the long-wavelength modes of the field describing the relative phase, ϕ , of the two components. In the perturbative regime, collective field excitations exhibit a relativistic dispersion with a tunable mass gap. We also observe explicitly non-perturbative phenomena, including the existence of topological domain walls across which ϕ rapidly winds by 2π (ref. 10 ). Our work opens possibilities for studies of cosmologically relevant phenomena including preheating 11,12 , dynamics of topological defects 13,14 and relativistic false-vacuum decay 15–19 .

articles.title: Fully integrated perovskite active polaritonic circuits
articles.titleEn: Fully integrated perovskite active polaritonic circuits
articles.abstract: Photonic integrated circuits are emerging as a key technology for compact, analogue and energy-efficient optical information processing 1 . Yet, their practical implementation remains limited by the intrinsically weak optical nonlinearities of conventional materials, which demand high power and large device footprints to achieve substantial nonlinear responses 2 . Exciton–polaritons, hybrid light–matter excitations of semiconducting materials, offer a promising route to overcome these limitations by combining strong optical nonlinearities with the high speed and scalability typical of photonic platforms 3–5 . However, despite their potential, fully integrated on-chip polaritonic systems simultaneously delivering room-temperature waveguide lasing, controllable optical routing and amplification have remained elusive. Here we demonstrate a fully integrated perovskite polaritonic circuit that brings these functionalities together in a single-step-grown platform. We realize precise and scalable polariton circuits with integrated gratings that act as both couplers and reflectors, enabling in-plane Fabry–Pérot cavities. These structures support robust in-plane polariton lasing with coherent guided emission at a geometry-defined wavelength, optical amplification of propagating polaritons and nonlinear optical phase control exceeding π, all within the same on-chip architecture. Our results establish perovskite polariton circuits as a scalable platform for active and interferometric integrated photonics.
