articles.title: Tropical land-use intensification restructures biodiversity
articles.titleEn: Tropical land-use intensification restructures biodiversity
articles.abstract: Tropical land-use intensification threatens global biodiversity, yet most assessments of tropical agricultural landscapes focus on local-scale biodiversity, overlooking how land use restructures biodiversity across space and multiple taxa. Here we provide an ecosystem-wide assessment of 24 taxonomic groups across all domains of life—encompassing 40,049 species—along a land-use intensification gradient from lowland forests to intensively managed smallholder cash-crop monocultures in Indonesian landscapes. Despite widespread losses of landscape and local multidiversity 1 in monocultures (approximately 78% and 50%, respectively), we found no evidence for consistent community homogenization with land-use intensification. Instead, monocultures exhibit a systematic shift from turnover to nestedness for aboveground taxa. Such patterns of differentiation may mask trajectories towards biotic homogenization via early stages of assemblage simplification. Biotic differentiation has the potential to partly mitigate biodiversity losses by positively affecting γ-diversity. This opens management options, including the conservation of existing remnants of traditional agriculture and the implementation of sustainable management practices 2–4 . Our results demonstrate that tropical land-use intensification restructures biodiversity not only through species loss, but also via a pervasive reorganization of community composition across trophic levels. Conserving tropical biodiversity, therefore, requires a multi-taxon, landscape-scale perspective that explicitly integrates agricultural land uses with the protection of natural and semi-natural habitats to reconcile agricultural production and conservation.

articles.title: Kuroshio Extension warming shaped by Gulf Stream variability via the Arctic atmosphere
articles.titleEn: Kuroshio Extension warming shaped by Gulf Stream variability via the Arctic atmosphere
articles.abstract: Recent unprecedented ocean warming has produced coherent sea surface temperature anomalies across the Northern Hemisphere extratropics. While the tropical Pacific is a natural source of North Pacific variability, the influence of the mid-latitude North Atlantic has remained poorly understood. Here we investigate whether Gulf Stream variability modulates Kuroshio Extension variability using 100-year idealized model simulations. We find that Gulf Stream variability remotely modulates Kuroshio Extension variability, explaining 13% of its internal sea surface temperature variance, whereas we find no evidence that Kuroshio variability similarly modulates the Gulf Stream. Positive Gulf Stream sea surface temperature anomalies excite a Northern Annular Mode-like atmospheric circulation response that weakens the Aleutian Low over the North Pacific. The resulting northward shift of the Kuroshio Extension enhances northward warm-water transport and promotes warming in the western mid-latitude North Pacific. We further show that a high-resolution ocean model is required to properly capture this coupling between Gulf Stream variability and atmospheric circulation, highlighting the importance of western boundary currents and associated oceanic fronts for this interbasin pathway. These findings indicate that North Atlantic variability contributed to the exceptional North Pacific warming during 2020–2024 and may provide a source of decadal predictability for Northern Hemisphere climate.

articles.title: Lake hydrochemistry and aquatic plant diversity across permafrost landscapes of Yakutia, Eastern Siberia
articles.titleEn: Lake hydrochemistry and aquatic plant diversity across permafrost landscapes of Yakutia, Eastern Siberia
articles.abstract: Central Yakutia in eastern Siberia is characterized by abundant lakes in permafrost-thaw depressions, named alaas. They constitute the traditional cultural landscape that is home to the indigenous Sakha people, providing critical ecosystem services. This study aims at assessing present-day lake characteristics and exploring their drivers based on lake hydrochemistry and aquatic and terrestrial plant diversity derived from sedimentary DNA in surface sediments. Macrophyte diversity reflects different lake types distinguished using both lake morphology and hydrochemistry. It also reveals a dominance of brackish water-tolerant cosmopolitan submerged macrophytes across all lakes, particularly Stuckenia and Potamogeton . In contrast, Myriophyllum and M. verticillatum are exclusively found in mountain lakes and freshwater lakes in the lowlands. The hydrochemical analysis reveals a clear distinction between low-mineralised mountain lakes and the highly variable hydrochemistry of the lowland lakes with much higher mineral content. Mountain lake hydrochemistry seems to be mainly determined by climate, whereas environmental drivers of hydrochemistry in lowland thermokarst lakes are more diverse. New thermokarst lakes are characterised by high dissolved organic carbon (DOC) and mainly located in forests. In contrast, connected alaas lakes, typically located in large alaas systems with settlements and active land use, display lower DOC and mineralisation, despite their location close to anthropogenic influence. We assume that temporary high discharge, such as during snowmelts, enables dilution, thus lowering organic and mineral contents. Future warming may lead to prolonged exposure to evaporation, but also to increased hydrological connectivity and increase in the number of connected alaas lakes, thereby potentially providing more freshwater to the region.

articles.title: Data‐Driven Flux Parameterization for the Atmospheric Boundary Layer
articles.titleEn: Data‐Driven Flux Parameterization for the Atmospheric Boundary Layer
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: Turbulent fluxes in the atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) govern the exchange of momentum, heat, and mass between the surface and the atmosphere, thereby shaping the vertical structure of the ABL and influencing a wide range of engineering applications, atmospheric processes, and boundary layer dynamics. Accurate parameterization of these fluxes in coarse‐resolution weather and climate models remains challenging, particularly under unstable conditions where flux transport is strongly nonlocal and under stable conditions where turbulence may become intermittent and partially decoupled from surface forcing. In this study, we develop a data‐driven parameterization of turbulent fluxes using a novel formulation in which nondimensional fluxes are represented as a linearized convolution operation acting on the relevant nondimensional mean‐state profiles. A comprehensive high‐resolution large eddy simulation (LES) data set is generated for idealized flow over homogeneous surfaces across a range of stability conditions. Using selected training cases from this data set, we derive and test several first‐order versions of this linearized convolution flux parameterization, each based on different combinations of inputs, that map mean temperature and velocity profiles to heat and momentum fluxes. The best‐performing parameterization is determined as the one that minimizes the mean squared error in both training cases and unseen testing cases. The results indicate that the proposed method improves predictive skill relative to commonly used closures (the standard K‐profile parameterization is used here as the benchmark) while preserving a transparent operator structure that can be inspected for physical meaning. Rather than treating the learned closure as a purely empirical mapping, the present framework learns flux–profile relationships as operators constrained by the governing column dynamics, enabling the inferred operator kernels to reveal the spatial organization and locality or nonlocality of turbulent transport across stability regimes. Despite being restricted to linear operators, the resulting parameterization remains interpretable, performs strongly across diverse stability conditions, and tests successfully in a posteriori single column model simulations, yielding state profiles that agree closely with the LES data.

articles.title: Testing the temporal and spatial transferability of a water balance model using a parameter learning approach
articles.titleEn: Testing the temporal and spatial transferability of a water balance model using a parameter learning approach
articles.abstract: Reliable transferability of hydrological model parameters across time and space remains a challenge for large-scale water resources assessment. In this study, we investigate whether a differentiable hybrid framework can identify robust and physically coherent parameter sets for annual streamflow modeling across a large-sample dataset of 3044 catchments from eight countries. To focus on temporal and spatial transferability analysis, we work at the annual time scale using what we consider to be the simplest possible model: an annual anomaly model of climate elasticities, coupled with the Turc–Mezentsev formulation for the long-term streamflow mean (MQ). A dense neural network is trained in an end-to-end fashion to map catchment descriptors to the four model parameters: because the anomaly-model equations are fully differentiable with respect to their parameters, the gradients of the streamflow loss are backpropagated through these equations to the neural network weights. We evaluate the framework using three cross-validation settings inspired by Klemeš (1986): temporal, spatial, and combined temporal–spatial cross-validation. As a benchmark, we compare the hybrid model against local, catchment-by-catchment linear regressions under temporal cross-validation. Our results show that, for temporal transferability, our parameter learning approach outperforms local calibration, yielding higher Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) values while producing elasticity coefficients that remain within plausible physical ranges, despite lacking explicit parameter constraints. By contrast, spatial transferability reveals a marked limitation: the anomaly component extrapolates well spatially, but regionalizing MQ from descriptors proves difficult, with MQ errors dominating the loss of performance in spatial and spatiotemporal cross-validation. Experiments with random descriptors further show that our parameter learning uses attributes mainly as catchment identifiers in temporal cross-validation but relies on their physical content to sustain spatial transfer, particularly for MQ. Overall, the study demonstrates that simple differentiable hybrid annual models can learn robust and interpretable anomaly parameters, while highlighting MQ regionalization as the main remaining bottleneck for spatially transferable annual streamflow predictions.

articles.title: Covariance-informed spatiotemporal clustering improves the detection of hazardous weather events
articles.titleEn: Covariance-informed spatiotemporal clustering improves the detection of hazardous weather events
articles.abstract: Spatiotemporal clustering can be used to detect weather events in multi-dimensional datasets. This method requires that the resolution of a dataset equivalently resolves variability across space and time, thereby normalizing the dataset for unbiased clustering across three dimensions. While spatiotemporal clustering is widely used, few studies quantitatively assess whether a dataset's resolution satisfies the normalization assumption required for unbiased clustering. To address this methodological gap, we present a framework to quantify the relationship between space and time using space time separable covariance modelling. We demonstrate that by defining a temporal resolution of interest (e.g., hours, days), the equivalent spatial resolution can be empirically derived using a space time metric. We present a case study using the unsupervised machine learning method Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN) to detect extreme heat and precipitation events across the Southeastern United States between 1940 and 2023 from ECMWF Reanalysis version 5 (ERA5) data. We analyse the behaviour of space time metrics for precipitation and heat index before selecting representative values. Our results indicate that both ERA5-derived heat index and precipitation are not sufficiently resolved at their native resolutions (i.e., 0.25 spatial degrees). We demonstrate that subsequently resampling the data by the space time metric often leads to small but significant increases in the F1 score for both extreme heat and precipitation events when compared against weather warnings reported to the Iowa Environmental Mesonet from 2002 to 2023. However, even after resampling, the model exhibits poor performance, suggesting that extreme weather events with relatively small footprints cannot be resolved in reanalysis data. Despite these findings, temporal geostatistics enable measurement of the daily variability in event structure across space and time, providing novel insights into the large-scale meteorological processes (e.g., weather regimes, climate patterns) influencing observed variability.

articles.title: To tip or not to tip
articles.titleEn: To tip or not to tip
articles.abstract: Tipping points have become a buzzword in Earth sciences, but ambiguous or overly narrow definitions of tipping are causing confusion around the concept. Agreeing on what tipping means, and whether a system tips or not, is important for robust science and communicating tipping risk. Based on a critical evaluation of existing tipping definitions, we propose a revised, general definition that characterizes a tipping event as a persistent nonlinear transition in forced systems. Our definition emphasizes both the phenomenology (observed time series) and cause (feedback mechanism) of a tipping event. Inspired by response theory, our proposition is compatible with more specific mathematical formulations while avoiding challenging notions such as bifurcations, equilibrium states, abruptness and irreversibility – making the definition testable also on transient dynamics in diverse complex systems under time-varying forcing. We showcase its practical use and limitations in a toy model and a case study of Earth system model data.

articles.title: Seasonal Asynchrony of Microbial Biomass and Respiration Across Terrestrial Ecosystems
articles.titleEn: Seasonal Asynchrony of Microbial Biomass and Respiration Across Terrestrial Ecosystems
articles.abstract: Soil microorganisms are fundamental drivers of terrestrial carbon cycling, acting both as a major reservoir of carbon through their biomass and as a dominant flux via respiration. While conventional models assume a positive correlation between microbial biomass and respiration at the interannual scale, the seasonal synchrony between these two components remains poorly understood. Here, we analyzed seasonal data from 323 studies to assess the synchrony between microbial biomass carbon and respiration, and used site‐level observations to explore the underlying mechanisms. We observed a seasonal asynchrony between microbial biomass and respiration, meaning that periods of higher biomass did not consistently coincide with higher respiration rates. This seasonal asynchrony was consistent with divergent governing mechanisms, in which microbial biomass was associated with plant competition, whereas microbial respiration was closely associated with temperature. Our findings provide correlative evidence to refine microbial‐mediated carbon seasonal dynamics in Earth system models under increasing climatic seasonality.

This seasonal asynchrony was consistent with divergent governing mechanisms, in which microbial biomass was associated with plant competition, whereas microbial respiration was closely associated with temperature. Our findings provide correlative evidence to refine microbial‐mediated carbon seasonal dynamics in Earth system models under increasing climatic seasonality.

articles.title: Near‐Term Anthropogenic Aerosol Reductions Under a Future Sustainability Pathway Could Avoid Nearly 40% of Mid‐Century PM 2.5 Mortality
articles.titleEn: Near‐Term Anthropogenic Aerosol Reductions Under a Future Sustainability Pathway Could Avoid Nearly 40% of Mid‐Century PM 2.5 Mortality
articles.abstract: Ambitious climate and air quality mitigation cuts anthropogenic aerosol emissions, lowering fine particulate matter (PM 2.5 ) and mortality, but the magnitude, regional distribution, and uncertainty of these reductions remain insufficiently quantified. Using nine Earth System Models from the Regional Aerosol Model Intercomparison Project (RAMIP), we quantify the PM 2.5 mortality benefits of switching anthropogenic aerosols alone from a low mitigation (SSP3‐7.0) to a high mitigation (SSP1‐2.6) scenario. The switch avoids 2.36 million (95% CI: 1.48–2.57 million) deaths/year globally in 2050, equivalent to 38% of SSP3‐7.0 PM 2.5 ‐attributable mortality. Benefits are largest in East Asia, South Asia, and Africa and smaller in North America and Europe. Global land annual mean PM 2.5 falls by 2%–17% across the RAMIP experiments, reaching 33%–38% near Asian sources. Cuts in East Asia alone avoid 48% of source region and 22% of global PM 2.5 mortality. Uncertainty is dominated by inter‐model variability, followed by health response functions and natural climate variability. Overall, sustainability‐pathway aerosol reductions can avoid nearly 40% of projected PM 2.5 deaths by 2050, with health benefits that are large but highly unevenly spatially distributed.

articles.title: City‐Wide Impacts of Cooling Infrastructure on Urban Outdoor Heat Stress of Populations With Diverse Physiological Characteristics
articles.titleEn: City‐Wide Impacts of Cooling Infrastructure on Urban Outdoor Heat Stress of Populations With Diverse Physiological Characteristics
articles.abstract: Adaptation strategies to reduce urban overheating are necessary to counteract rising trends in population exposure to extreme heat and associated health issues. The impact of these strategies has been traditionally assessed using only surface or air temperature ( T a ), but some of these strategies may involve trade‐offs and need to be evaluated using more comprehensive metrics. In this study, we combine a physiologically‐based human heat balance model with a mesoscale meteorological model developed for outdoor thermal exposure to assess the impacts of street trees and cool (reflective) roofs, walls and pavement on heat stress across diverse populations. The study focuses on the hot and arid Las Vegas Valley and considers five representative personal profiles that combine different physical and behavioral characteristics. All strategies reduce daytime T a , but radiation effects dominate, leading to contrasting impacts on human heat stress across metrics. Street trees produce the smallest T a reductions but the largest heat stress benefit due to shade provision. In contrast, reflective walls and pavements increase heat stress by reflecting radiation toward pedestrians, even though they produce larger T a reductions. Under the assumption of continuous outdoor exposure, we find large differences across population groups, with the more sensitive profiles experiencing over twice as many hours of uncompensable heat stress relative to young individuals. Our results highlight the importance of considering context‐specific profiles and examining the different avenues of heat exchange on humans when assessing the impacts of cooling strategies on urban overheating and heat stress.

articles.title: Mitigating Non‐Stationarity in Machine Learning–Based Downscaling of Climate Projections
articles.titleEn: Mitigating Non‐Stationarity in Machine Learning–Based Downscaling of Climate Projections
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: Machine learning (ML) models perform well for climate downscaling when training and testing data follow similar statistical distributions. However, their performance can degrade as future climate statistics depart from the historical training record. We systematically investigate this problem by downscaling global temperature and precipitation fields across multiple emission pathways and two solar radiation modification (SRM) scenarios in the Max Planck Institute Earth System Model, comparing four machine learning configurations with bilinear interpolation and quantile delta mapping (QDM). A baseline ML model trained on the historical period degrades substantially under future forcing, reaching a global mean temperature error of 1.6C by 2100 under SSP5‐8.5. Preprocessing the ML model's input and target to reduce non‐stationarity via detrending and residual correction keeps the global mean error within 0.2C, comparable to that of QDM. All downscaling methods compared here show substantially lower skill when evaluated on anomalies rather than total fields, suggesting that much of their skill comes from correcting the climatological mean. QDM better preserves precipitation extremes and fine‐scale variance, whereas the ML models have lower pointwise errors. Downscaling the SRM scenarios produces larger spatial temperature biases than the emission pathways. We also generate 0.25 monthly temperature projections for G6sulfur, providing a benchmark for future regional downscaling studies.

articles.title: Resolution Controls on SST–Precipitation Coupling in Western Boundary Currents
articles.titleEn: Resolution Controls on SST–Precipitation Coupling in Western Boundary Currents
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: Western boundary currents (WBCs) are hotspots of air–sea interaction where observations show strong local covariability between sea surface temperature (SST) and precipitation anomalies. We investigate how oceanic and atmospheric horizontal resolution, mesoscale SST variability, and the treatment of atmospheric convection control this coupling across the Gulf Stream, Kuroshio, Agulhas, and Brazil currents. Using a coordinated hierarchy of ICON and EC‐Earth3P model simulations spanning horizontal resolutions of about 5–100 km, either parameterizing or explicitly simulating atmospheric convection, complementary atmosphere‐only sensitivity experiments forced with mesoscale‐resolving or smoothed SSTs, and the CMIP6 ensemble, we assess how model design impacts the strength and spatial structure of SST–precipitation covariability. Resolving mesoscale SST variability is necessary to reproduce the observed localized precipitation responses, but a high horizontal resolution alone does not guarantee full realism. Overly broad coupling emerges in simulations with 5–25 km oceanic resolutions, while explicitly simulating atmospheric convection at 10 km atmospheric resolution produces weaker, more spatially confined precipitation responses than parameterized convection. Whereas mesoscale SST variability sets the potential for strong SST–precipitation coupling, atmospheric physics controls the efficiency of the precipitation response. Our results emphasize the importance of both increasing model resolution and improving its physics for representing realistic air–sea coupling in next‐generation climate simulations.

articles.title: Drought May Alter the Flux of Essential Omega‐3 Fatty Acids From Streams to Terrestrial Ecosystems
articles.titleEn: Drought May Alter the Flux of Essential Omega‐3 Fatty Acids From Streams to Terrestrial Ecosystems
articles.abstract: Stream and riparian food webs are connected via cross‐ecosystem subsidies, including essential nutrients like omega‐3 fatty acids that originate in the aquatic environment (microalgae) but support terrestrial consumers. Although global change stressors could be disrupting these linkages, most research to date has focused on subsidy quantity rather than quality. Here, we reviewed the literature on omega‐3 long‐chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (ω3 LC‐PUFA) in streams and other freshwaters, and we examined how drought‐related stress may influence their production, accumulation, and trophic transfer. Although direct evidence linking drought conditions to changes in stream ω3 LC‐PUFA dynamics is limited, existing studies point to several disruptive mechanisms: warming‐ and drying‐induced shifts in basal resource composition and primary production, altered consumer community composition and emergence phenology, and reduced capacity for ω3 LC‐PUFA bioconversion. ω3 LC‐PUFA accumulation in organisms is driven primarily by species identity and further shaped by life‐history traits such as drought adaptations (e.g., resistance and resilience strategies), temporal integration of diet, and feeding ecology. We explored these mechanisms via a case study on intermittent stream invertebrates at Pinnacles National Park, California, and found largely taxon‐specific patterns rather than consistent responses to hydrology. Finally, we identified key challenges and recommendations for advancing ω3 LC‐PUFA research. These include (i) explicitly considering organismal life histories; (ii) improving sampling design to strengthen inference; (iii) considering underground ecological processes; (iv) advancing research on consumer fitness responses to ω3 LC‐PUFA limitation and on “upgrading”; (v) measuring rates and fluxes; and (vi) scaling up and forecasting fatty acid flux under increasingly dry futures by integrating models of hydrology, organismal biology, and community dynamics. We contend that the disruption of cross‐ecosystem linkages, not just in resource magnitude but also in quality, is a “blind spot” of global change ecology that demands immediate attention.

articles.title: Belowground Productivity in Grasslands and Savannas Depends on Shifting Fire and Herbivory Regimes
articles.titleEn: Belowground Productivity in Grasslands and Savannas Depends on Shifting Fire and Herbivory Regimes
articles.abstract: In grasslands and savannas, most plant biomass and net primary productivity is belowground. How shifts in disturbance regimes, such as fire or large herbivore activity, impact belowground net primary productivity (BNPP) is unclear across climate‐driven productivity gradients. We tested the hypothesis that altered fire and herbivory regimes impact BNPP by changing the relative biomass of herbaceous and woody plants, which differ in their relative allocation to BNPP, and that climate constrains how much disturbance shifts this herbaceous–woody balance. We measured BNPP and aboveground vegetation across seven African and North American grasslands and savannas, with three long‐term fire manipulation levels (high frequency, intermediate frequency, and suppressed) and, at six sites, two long‐term herbivory levels (large herbivores excluded or open to large herbivores). Sites spanned an aridity index (mean annual precipitation [mm]/potential evapotranspiration [mm]) gradient—and associated woody thickening potential—from 0.21 to 0.71. BNPP increased with water availability. Fire and herbivory increased BNPP, with greater effects in wetter sites. In the wettest sites, BNPP gains under disturbance correlated with herbaceous biomass gains, as herbivory and frequent fire reduced woody plant cover relative to disturbance exclusion plots. BNPP responses were also predicted by root biomass, explaining why wetter sites and frequently disturbed plots within sites had higher BNPP. Climate determined how much the positive response of root biomass offset fire and grazing reductions in aboveground plant stocks, largely because water availability constrained the total aboveground plant biomass achieved without disturbance. Therefore, disturbances stimulated BNPP in wet savannas, largely by limiting woody thickening and promoting herbaceous growth with higher BNPP rates, whereas BNPP in drier and mesic sites tended to be resilient. Our findings show that belowground processes in grasslands and savannas fundamentally depend on disturbance regimes, climate‐driven productivity gradients, and their interactions, with important implications for understanding global carbon storage.

articles.title: Improving Global Simulation of Irrigation Within the Land Information System
articles.titleEn: Improving Global Simulation of Irrigation Within the Land Information System
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: Irrigated agriculture increases evapotranspiration and near surface humidity, decreases air and ground temperatures, augments downwind precipitation, enhances recharge, and depletes surface water and/or groundwater resources. However, model developers have been slow to incorporate irrigation. Using the latest satellite‐based land cover and irrigation data sets and innovative modeling approaches, we developed a scheme for simulating irrigation in the Land Information System (LIS). We reconciled global and national irrigation, land cover, and crop class databases in an effort to (a) distinguish irrigated and rainfed agriculture, (b) approximate fractional crop cover in each model grid pixel, and (c) apply the most likely irrigation method based on the crop class and country or state level information on the relative usage of sprinkler, furrow, paddy, and drip irrigation. Each irrigation method is represented by a separate algorithm. We used agricultural water withdrawal data, as available, for calibration and evaluation. The results compare favorably with available observational and reported data in terms of patterns. The simulated mean annual global irrigation rate, 2,765 km 3 /yr, is on par with an observational estimate (2,500 km 3 /yr) and other irrigation simulating models (mean 2,700 km 3 /yr). Over the contiguous U.S., based on county level reported irrigation water usage data, the new scheme had a root mean square error of 0.22 km 3 while correctly simulating the occurrence of irrigation in 3,053 of 3,220 irrigated counties, compared with 0.24 km 3 /yr and 2,334 counties for LIS's original scheme. Irrigation is estimated to increase global evapotranspiration by 1,700 km 3 /yr (2.4%), similar to a recent independent estimate.

articles.title: Antiferroelectric hafnia down to the 2D limit
articles.titleEn: Antiferroelectric hafnia down to the 2D limit
articles.abstract: Antiferroelectricity is a material property characterized by alternating electric dipoles spontaneously ordered in antiparallel directions. Antiferroelectrics are promising for energy storage, solid-state cooling, and memory technologies; however, these materials are scarce, and their scalability remains largely unexplored. In this work, we demonstrated that single-crystalline hafnia, a lead-free complementary metal-oxide semiconductor (CMOS)–compatible material, exhibits antiferroelectricity under compressive-strain conditions. We observed antiparallel sublattice polarization and stable double hysteresis in single-crystalline (111)-oriented epitaxial lanthanum (La)–doped hafnia films grown on yttrium-stabilized zirconia and showed that the antipolar orthorhombic phase of hafnia adheres to the Kittel model of antiferroelectricity. Compressive strain strengthens the orthorhombic order in thinner La-doped hafnia films, achieving a very high ordering temperature of 850°C in the two-dimensional limit, highlighting hafnia’s potential for advanced antiferroelectric devices.

articles.title: Poisoned hunting weapons, megafauna, and plant use at a 125,000-year-old Arabian paleolakeshore
articles.titleEn: Poisoned hunting weapons, megafauna, and plant use at a 125,000-year-old Arabian paleolakeshore
articles.abstract: After the African origin of Homo sapiens , multiple dispersals radiated into Asia, yet the Saharo-Arabian archaeological record remains sparse. In this study, we report on ‘Uruq Aljelibah, a Middle Paleolithic site dated to ~125,000 years ago (marine isotope stage 5e) and located on the shore of Mundafan paleolake, Saudi Arabia. Levallois assemblages, refits, and megafaunal associations indicate in situ tool production and carcass processing. Stone tool residues, use-wear, and biomarkers reveal animal and plant processing, including palms, tubers, trees, and shrubs. Several points exhibit impact damage and poison residues (from Acokanthera schimperi ), indicating use as hafted weapon tips within composite hunting systems. Megafaunal remains include hippopotamus, buffalo, gazelle, ostrich, and camel, illuminating hominin use of freshwater and grassland ecosystems.

articles.title: Combining different views on internal climate variability of temperature over Europe
articles.titleEn: Combining different views on internal climate variability of temperature over Europe
articles.abstract: Internal climate variability (ICV) represents the intrinsic fluctuations within the climate system. Understanding how ICV varies across regions, seasons, and climatic conditions is crucial for detecting externally forced climate change and assessing future climate risks. It can also provide a useful benchmark for assessing climate model performance and the emergence of anthropogenically forced climate change. This study aims to compare ICV estimates obtained using different methods and data types. We focus on seasonal mean near-surface air temperature over Europe, utilizing data from 15 CMIP6 models, a 100-member MPI-ESM large ensemble, and three observational datasets. The ICV estimates are based on pre-industrial control simulations (Pidata), the Hawkins and Sutton (2009) residual-based method (HS09), regression-based removal of external forcings, and a single-model large-ensemble framework. The magnitude of ICV estimates generally decreases from northeastern to southwestern Europe on both annual and seasonal timescales, except during JJA, when the highest estimates shift southward. The highest ICV estimates are observed in DJF and the lowest at the annual timescale. Among all the methods, Pidata generally yields the highest ICV estimates across all seasonal and annual timescales, except during JJA. Based on the HS09 method, the similarity between the model-based estimates and the observations is most pronounced during DJF and at the annual timescale. However, this similarity is weaker when the regression-based method is applied, with the model-based estimates generally exceeding the observation-based ones. The projected changes in ICV show a tendency for reduced (enhanced) values in DJF (JJA). Although a north-south contrast emerges in other seasons, with declining (increasing) ICV in northern (southern) Europe, the overall spatial pattern indicates a reduction in projected ICV estimates across large parts of Europe, except during JJA.

articles.title: Three‐Phase Mobilization of Organic Phosphorus Sustains Phosphorus Bioavailability Under Long‐Term Nitrogen Addition in a Subtropical Plantation
articles.titleEn: Three‐Phase Mobilization of Organic Phosphorus Sustains Phosphorus Bioavailability Under Long‐Term Nitrogen Addition in a Subtropical Plantation
articles.abstract: Nitrogen (N) input is expected to intensify phosphorus (P) limitation in tropical and subtropical forests. However, how soil and microbial processes mobilize P from poorly available pools to sustain soil P bioavailability remains unclear. We conducted a nine‐year experiment with low (20 kg N ha −1 year −1 ) and high (80 kg N ha −1 year −1 ) N addition treatments in a subtropical Moso bamboo ( Phyllostachys edulis ) plantation. We quantified soil P fractions, P‐cycling functional genes, phosphatase activity, P sorption capacity (PSC), iron and aluminum oxides, and plant properties throughout the experiment. Our results reveal three distinct stages in the regulation of soil bioavailable P with prolonged N addition. Phase I: N addition reduces P bioavailability, and labile organic P decomposition becomes the main source of bioavailable P, associated with increased phosphatase activity. Phase II: when labile organic P becomes insufficient to meet P demand, bioavailable P is replenished through the depletion of moderately labile organic P; this is related to decreased PSC and enhanced acid phosphomonoesterases activity. Phase III: stable organic P decreases significantly, jointly sustaining bioavailable P with the depletion of other organic P fractions, alongside a further decrease in PSC and enriched microbial organic acid‐ and phosphatase‐related genes. This study uncovers a novel “three‐phased P supply” model revealed through long‐term observations. These mechanistic insights reveal the pathways of soil P mobilization under continuous N input in a subtropical forest and establish a framework for predicting the buffering capacity of soil P pools in P‐limited ecosystems under global change scenarios.

However, how soil and microbial processes mobilize P from poorly available pools to sustain soil P bioavailability remains unclear. We quantified soil P fractions, P‐cycling functional genes, phosphatase activity, P sorption capacity (PSC), iron and aluminum oxides, and plant properties throughout the experiment. Our results reveal three distinct stages in the regulation of soil bioavailable P with prolonged N addition. Phase I: N addition reduces P bioavailability, and labile organic P decomposition becomes the main source of bioavailable P, associated with increased phosphatase activity. Phase II: when labile organic P becomes insufficient to meet P demand, bioavailable P is replenished through the depletion of moderately labile organic P; this is related to decreased PSC and enhanced acid phosphomonoesterases activity. Phase III: stable organic P decreases significantly, jointly sustaining bioavailable P with the depletion of other organic P fractions, alongside a further decrease in PSC and enriched microbial organic acid‐ and phosphatase‐related genes. This study uncovers a novel “three‐phased P supply” model revealed through long‐term observations. These mechanistic insights reveal the pathways of soil P mobilization under continuous N input in a subtropical forest and establish a framework for predicting the buffering capacity of soil P pools in P‐limited ecosystems under global change scenarios.

articles.title: Mineral‐Associated Carbon Accrual Masks Labile Particulate Carbon Loss in Permafrost Region on the Tibetan Plateau
articles.titleEn: Mineral‐Associated Carbon Accrual Masks Labile Particulate Carbon Loss in Permafrost Region on the Tibetan Plateau
articles.abstract: Permafrost regions store vast quantities of soil organic carbon (SOC), yet the future trajectories of functionally distinct SOC fractions across soil depths remain poorly constrained. Integrating depth‐explicit soil fractionation data from 104 sites across the Tibetan permafrost region with a process‐based SOC model, we project century‐scale dynamics of particulate (POC) and mineral‐associated organic carbon (MAOC) under three emission scenarios. We show that MAOC currently comprises 56.5% of regional total SOC stock and remains far from saturation throughout the profile. Consistent with this large stabilization capacity, total SOC was projected to increase over the 21st century under all scenarios, with the largest gains under SSP5‐8.5. However, this positive net gain masked a significant restructuring of SOC fractions. MAOC accumulated across all depths and scenarios, and heavy POC remained comparatively buffered, whereas light POC declined under SSP5‐8.5. The strongest relative light POC losses occurred in the 10–30 cm layers, where warming‐driven decomposition remained strong while plant‐C input compensation weakened. These divergent trajectories indicate a shift toward a “carbon‐rich yet energy‐poor” state, where mineral‐bound carbon increases while the labile particulate pool supporting microbial activity is depleted. Our findings reveal SOC vulnerability in permafrost region is governed by both fraction identity and soil depth, and that net SOC gains can conceal the loss of metabolically active carbon. Incorporating measurable, depth‐resolved SOC fractions into Earth system models is therefore essential for constraining permafrost–climate feedbacks.

articles.title: Intensive Agriculture and Erosion Affect Composition of Soil Organic Matter
articles.titleEn: Intensive Agriculture and Erosion Affect Composition of Soil Organic Matter
articles.abstract: Land‐use changes induced by human activities usually accelerate soil erosion, leading to losses of soil organic matter (SOM). The mechanisms by which cultivation‐associated degradation affects SOM composition via changes of content and quality of particulate (POM), mineral‐associated (MAOM), dissolved organic matter (DOM), and microbial biomass are not elucidated. We investigated the C:N stoichiometry of these fractions, and erosion (using 137 Cs activity) along a chronosequence of cultivation‐associated degradation (0–114 years) in Mollisols. Two‐pool and Bayesian three‐source mixing models estimated contributions of microbial biomass, DOM, and POM to MAOM to the total SOM. Erosion intensity ranged locally from 440 to 4800 t km −2 year −1 , resulting in cumulative soil losses of 11,000 to 320,000 t km −2 over 114 years of cultivation. As cultivation duration and eroded amounts increased, the C/N ratios of POM, MAOM, and DOM declined owing to (i) the faster loss of C than N, (ii) a decrease in C/N with soil depth involved in tillage horizon, and (iii) N input by fertilization. These higher C than N losses reflect that erosion is not the sole process leading to the decline of C stocks, but intensive cultivation also accelerates organic matter mineralization and CO 2 release to the atmosphere. As the C/N ratios of POM and MAOM declined but microbial C/N increased, the estimated contribution of microbial inputs to MAOM increased from 6% to 32%. The Bayesian model partitioned MAOM sources into DOM (8%), microbial (11%), and POM (81%), reinforcing that POM dominates MAOM formation in croplands. Cultivation‐associated degradation led to SOC losses by reducing POM‐C/N and MAOM‐C/N ratios, while erosion strongly accelerated these effects. Furthermore, cultivation‐associated degradation is also based on the limited inputs of organic C as the precursors for MAOM formation by depleting POM. These results from a > 100‐year chronosequence indicate that cultivation‐induced degradation reduces SOM content, while also shifting the MAOM composition progressively towards a greater contribution of microbial C.

articles.title: A further acceleration of clean energy is needed for global CO2 emissions to peak and decline
articles.titleEn: A further acceleration of clean energy is needed for global CO2 emissions to peak and decline
articles.abstract: Global fossil fuel CO 2 emissions have grown 0.8% per year on average between 2019 and 2025. Here we project a decrease of 0.4% in 2026, probably as a short-term response to the energy shock triggered by the Iran conflict. Electric vehicles and solar and wind power offset about 64–79% of increasing emissions from demand growth through 2028; acceleration in clean technology deployment is needed to guarantee emissions peak and subsequent decline.

articles.title: Protected Areas Reduce Heat Exposure in Squamates Globally
articles.titleEn: Protected Areas Reduce Heat Exposure in Squamates Globally
articles.abstract: Protected areas (PAs) are central to biodiversity conservation, yet their capacity to buffer species from climate‐driven heat exposure, that is, the duration and frequency of exposure to temperatures exceeding species' critical thermal limits, remains poorly quantified at global scales. Here, we assessed whether squamate reptiles inside PAs experience lower heat exposure than conspecifics in unprotected, human‐modified landscapes, and how this buffering effect varies across latitudes, biomes, and evolutionary lineages. Using biophysical modelling of operative temperatures across 248 species, we show that PAs consistently reduced both annual hours above critical thermal maximum (CT max ) and the frequency of critical days under current and future climatic scenarios (+2°C and + 4°C). We found that under current climate, protected sites had 51 fewer hours above CT max and 3.5 fewer critical days than unprotected sites, and the proportional reduction persisted under +2°C and + 4°C warming scenarios. The buffering effect was most pronounced at low latitudes and tropical biomes, where species already operate close to their thermal limits. Deserts and xeric shrublands, together with tropical grasslands and savannas, emerged as biomes with elevated heat exposure, reinforcing growing concern for arid‐zone reptiles under climate change. Substantial phylogenetic signal in heat exposure indicated that evolutionary history shapes thermal vulnerability beyond geography and biome alone, with the magnitude of PA buffering varying considerably across squamate lineages. Our findings demonstrate that PAs can provide refugia from heat exposure, and that their conservation value under climate change depends on the retention of structurally complex habitats and thermally heterogeneous microhabitats.

articles.title: Using Artificial Intelligence to Optimize Ecological Restoration for Climate and Biodiversity
articles.titleEn: Using Artificial Intelligence to Optimize Ecological Restoration for Climate and Biodiversity
articles.abstract: The restoration of degraded ecosystems is critical for mitigating climate change and reversing biodiversity loss. Depending on the primary objective—such as maximizing carbon sequestration or protecting threatened species—and within the boundaries of budget limitations, different spatial priorities have been identified at global and regional scales. Funding mechanisms to support such work comprise public sources, philanthropy, and the private sector, including the sale of carbon and biodiversity credits. However, effectively exploring trade‐offs among restoration objectives and estimating the price of biodiversity and carbon credits to design financially viable projects remains scientifically challenging. Here we harness the power of artificial intelligence implemented in the software CAPTAIN to identify spatial priorities for ecological restoration that maximize multiple objectives at once and to allow a robust evaluation of biodiversity and climate outcomes. We find through a series of simulations that even low‐to‐moderate consideration of biodiversity in the design of restoration projects leads to the selection of restored areas that disproportionately improve the conservation of threatened species, while the carbon captured is only slightly reduced. We propose the bundling of biodiversity and carbon credits to support restoration efforts even in areas previously excluded for economic reasons. Applying our methodology to plant diversity in the Atlantic Forest of eastern South America, one of the most biodiverse and threatened ecosystems globally, we demonstrate its potential to guide restoration and to quantify trade‐offs between multiple optimization scenarios. Our study provides a robust, scalable method to maximize the joint benefits of ecological restoration for climate and nature.

articles.title: Past and future projected radiative effects from irrigation
articles.titleEn: Past and future projected radiative effects from irrigation
articles.abstract: Irrigation is the most dominant freshwater use practice on Earth, yet its effect on the top-of-atmosphere (TOA) radiative budget remains uncertain because past estimates have relied on idealised experiments or single-model frameworks. Here, we use historical simulations (1902–2014) from the Irrigation Model Intercomparison Project (IRRMIP) to provide the first multi-model quantification of irrigation-induced effective radiative forcing (ERF), defined as the change in net TOA radiative flux including rapid atmospheric adjustments. Across seven Earth system models, under prescribed sea surface temperatures (SST), the global multi-model mean (MMM) irrigation-induced ERF is positive but small (∼ 0.023 W m −2 ). While the global signal is small, it masks regional heterogeneity: South Asia and West Central Asia exhibit higher positive ERF (∼0.23 W m −2 ), with spatial maps revealing coherent forcing hotspots of up to +5 W m −2 over the Indo-Gangetic Plain that are consistent across all models, while East Asia shows negative ERF (∼-0.03 W m −2 ). The clear-sky ERF is greater than the all-sky ERF in most of the regions, indicating that cloud adjustments following irrigation may exert a negative contribution to the ERF. Correlations between historical irrigation ERF variability and its potential drivers suggest that reduced outgoing longwave radiation is the dominant control at the global scale, as well as in South Asia and West Central Asia, while near-surface temperature, precipitable water, albedo, and cloud cover contribute with substantial regional and inter-model variability. We additionally examine future changes in net TOA radiation imbalance (Δ R n,TOA ) from a fully coupled CMIP-style model (SSP1-2.6 and SSP3-7.0, 2015–2070) to assess whether the historical ERF pattern persists under future irrigation. The global mean Δ R n,TOA is more positive under the high irrigation demand pathway (SSP3-7.0) than under SSP1-2.6, consistent with projected differences in irrigation expansion between scenarios. These results demonstrate that irrigation's radiative influence, while small in the global mean, is regionally substantial and scenario-dependent, with implications for the attribution of regional climate change and for the design of land-based mitigation trajectories.

articles.title: Global-scale meteorological-to-groundwater drought propagation and the drivers and patterns of multi-year groundwater drought
articles.titleEn: Global-scale meteorological-to-groundwater drought propagation and the drivers and patterns of multi-year groundwater drought
articles.abstract: Groundwater stores a third of all global freshwater and supports water supply, irrigation and ecosystems across the world. As such, groundwater drought can have wide-reaching financial, social and environmental impacts, particularly when drought events are prolonged or multi-year. Although recent work has made significant progress in understanding the drivers and patterns of multi-year meteorological droughts, we do not know how this signal translates into multi-year groundwater drought, where subsurface processes, anthropogenic influences and abstractions can alter the meteorological signal. This is particularly true at the global-scale, where a major barrier to understanding large-scale groundwater drought dynamics is the difficulty of obtaining consistent and comprehensive groundwater data. In this research, we use a new global hyper-resolution (∼1 km) groundwater dataset to investigate the global patterns and drivers of groundwater drought from 1960–2019, with a specific focus on multi-year events. We start by characterizing the propagation of meteorological (represented by SPEI-12) to groundwater drought, evaluating how and to what extent the sub-surface plays a role in modulating the meteorological drought signal. Subsequently, we define three global groundwater response types that provide a framework for understanding the processes and geo-physical drivers of normal versus multi-year groundwater droughts. We find that 35 % of global groundwater grid cells have an average groundwater drought duration which is multi-year. In 83 % of these locations, the subsurface extends the meteorological drought signal, whereas in the remaining 17 %, groundwater drought duration appears to be primarily driven by meteorological anomalies. Our analysis offers new insights into global-scale drought exposure by identifying regions which have been most vulnerable to multi-year groundwater drought in the past, as well as those which might be more vulnerable in the future. Importantly, our typology also highlights areas where multi-year groundwater droughts can be anticipated based on meteorological drought anomalies and can therefore inform strategies for managing and mitigating future water scarcity risks.

articles.title: On combining climate models into weighted ensembles
articles.titleEn: On combining climate models into weighted ensembles
articles.abstract: Several methods have been proposed and used to refine estimates of future climate change based on combined output from comprehensive climate models. While previously the so-called model democracy approach was used to combine model outputs, where every model is given equal weight, it is now widely accepted that using model weights that account for model performance and model independence is necessary to obtain more reliable results. However, most existing approaches rely, implicitly or explicitly, on a similar statistical basis, while describing things in different ways. Here we distinguish between approaches that are based on the performance of individual models (individual performance weighting) and approaches that are based on the performance of the weighted ensemble as a whole (ensemble performance weighting). At the same time, we formulate both in probabilistic Bayesian terms to make their application and comparison straightforward. Using simple constructed examples, we demonstrate that the ensemble performance weighting approach implicitly accounts for co-dependencies among models, which arguably makes the computation of independence weights for the purpose of model weighting obsolete. We also show that a set of weighted models within the ensemble weighting approach will naturally tend to artificially reduce uncertainty and that this is strongly influenced by the choice of the prior distribution over weight vectors. The distinction between individual and ensemble performance weighting is both methodological and conceptual. Formulating both approaches in general probabilistic Bayesian terms as done here, can serve as a common basis for future developments with regard to ensemble model weighting in Earth system science. The discussed concepts are generally applicable across domains and are thus possibly relevant for other modeling communities as well.
